ox: Correct. Intersectionality, from Kimberlé Crenshaw, says identities like race, gender and class interact. The experience they create together isn't just the sum of each part.
Not quite. If each form of inequality worked independently, you could just add them up. Intersectionality's whole point is that they interact, so this denies the concept.
Not quite. Intersectionality looks at several categories working together, like race, gender, class and sexuality. Saying inequality is mainly economic boils it down to one.
Not quite. Sociologists, including those who use intersectionality, see race as socially constructed: its meaning comes from society, not biology. This contradicts that view.

p: Intersectionality is the idea that a person's social categories, like race, gender and class, overlap and interact. Kimberlé Crenshaw introduced the term.

The result is a distinct experience of disadvantage or privilege. A Black woman, for example, may face discrimination that differs from what Black men or white women face. On the MCAT, look for the answer that says the categories interact, not that they simply add up.

mem: Coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw
Identities overlap and interact; effects don't just add up
Race and gender are social constructs
d_10A_17.trap: Treating each category as a separate layer that simply stacks on the others.
d_10A_17.plain: Mixing blue and yellow paint doesn't give you a bit of blue next to a bit of yellow. It gives you green, something new.

ox: Not quite. Marx's alienation is about the workplace, not family life. Families aren't what workers are cut off from in his idea.
Not quite. Marx focused on what happens inside production, meaning how goods get made. Alienation isn't about workers' relationship to the government.

Correct. Under capitalism, workers don't control their labor and don't own what they make. Marx said this cuts them off from the work itself, the products, their fellow workers and their human potential.
Not quite. Feeling cut loose from society's norms sounds like anomie, Durkheim's term for normlessness when rules break down. That's a different idea from Marx's alienation.

p: Alienation means workers feel cut off because they don't control their work. They sell their labor to owners and don't own what they make.

Marx described four parts: alienation from the product, from the work process, from fellow workers and from their own human potential. It comes from how the economy is set up, not from a personal mood.

mem: Alienation: from labor, product, coworkers, human potential
Caused by how capitalist work is organized
Don't confuse it with Durkheim's anomie (normlessness)
d_10A_34.trap: Treating alienation as a mood rather than a result of how work is organized.
d_10A_34.plain: Picture a kid who builds toys on an assembly line all day and never gets to see or play with a finished one. They'd feel disconnected from the work.

ox: Not quite. There's no good evidence that social classes differ in built-in ability. Blaming biology for class gaps is called biological determinism, and sociologists reject it.
Not quite. Studies show poor families generally value education highly. Blaming their values is called a cultural deficit explanation, and it doesn't fit the evidence.
Not quite. The age kids start school doesn't differ much by class and doesn't explain the gaps sociologists see.

Correct. Unequal school funding, along with differences in family resources like books, tutoring and stable housing, gives some children built-in advantages. Most sociologists see this as the main source of class gaps.

p: Sociologists look at structure, meaning how society is set up. In much of the US, schools rely partly on local property taxes, so richer areas get better-funded schools.
Family resources, like books at home, tutoring and stable housing, add to this. The gaps come from unequal opportunity, not from a lack of talent or interest.

School funding often depends on local property taxes
Avoid explanations that blame the individual or culture
d_10A_37.trap: Blaming individual or cultural shortcomings instead of differences in resources.
d_10A_37.plain: Two kids race, but one gets good shoes and a smooth track. The gap comes from the gear, not the kids.

ox: Correct. Residential segregation means groups live apart, in different neighborhoods of the same area. It's about the pattern of who lives where.

Not quite. Gentrification happens when higher-income people move into a lower-income neighborhood, rents rise, and longtime residents get priced out. It's a process of change, not a description of groups living apart.
Not quite. Suburbanization is the movement of people out of central cities and into the suburbs around them. It can feed segregation, but the term itself just describes that move.

Not quite. Urban renewal is a policy of redeveloping run-down city areas, often by clearing old housing and building new projects. It's something done to a neighborhood, not the pattern of groups living apart.

p: Residential segregation is a pattern in which racial or ethnic groups live in different neighborhoods within the same metropolitan area. It's about where people live, not just how they feel about each other.

It was built up by discriminatory lending (like redlining), zoning rules and housing choices. It matters for health and life chances because where you live shapes your schools, jobs, safety and access to services.

mem: Residential segregation: groups split up by neighborhood
Gentrification: wealthier newcomers push out residents
Redlining helped create segregation
x10A_001.trap: Choosing gentrification just because it also changes neighborhoods.
x10A_001.plain: If every grade in a school ate lunch at its own set of tables, the cafeteria would be segregated by seating.

ox: Not quite. Anti-gentrification groups also work in lower-income neighborhoods, which is what makes this tempting. But their fight is about displacement: wealthier people move in, rents rise, and longtime residents get priced out. Where hazardous waste gets dumped is a different issue.

Correct. Environmental justice is about how pollution and environmental hazards get spread across a society. Research keeps finding that waste sites, highways and polluting plants land more often in low-income and majority-minority neighborhoods. This movement says that's unfair and pushes to share those burdens, and the benefits like parks and clean air, more evenly.
Not quite. Meritocracy is the idea that jobs, grades and rewards should go to people based on talent and effort. It has nothing to say about where hazardous waste facilities are built.

Not quite. Deinstitutionalization was the shift, starting in the mid-1900s, of moving people with mental illness out of large psychiatric hospitals and into community care. It's a real sociology term, but it isn't about pollution.

p: Environmental justice is a movement built on a simple idea: everyone should get a fair share of both the good things in the environment (clean air, parks, safe water) and the bad things (pollution, waste, noise). Study after study has found that hazards like landfills, highways and factories end up far more often near poor and minority communities.

When race in particular drives that pattern, people call it environmental racism. On the MCAT, this topic falls under social inequality: it's a clear example of how where you live shapes your health. Don't confuse it with gentrification, which is about rising costs pushing people out of a neighborhood.

x10A_002.trap: Picking anti-gentrification just because it's also about poorer neighborhoods. The question is about pollution, not rent.
x10A_002.plain: If the town dump always got built next to the same neighborhood, that wouldn't be fair, and the people living there would speak up. That's environmental justice.
mem: Environmental justice: unfair exposure to pollution by race and income
Gentrification: people priced out by rising costs
Deinstitutionalization: moving psychiatric patients out of hospitals

ox: Wrong. No known DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a 5' end. The direction is 5' to 3'. Trap: confusing the direction of the template read with the direction of the new strand.
Correct. DNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the free 3'-OH of the growing strand. So the new strand grows 5' to 3'. It reads the template 3' to 5'.
Wrong. Both leading and lagging strands are built 5' to 3'. The lagging strand just has to be built in short Okazaki fragments away from the fork.
Wrong. DNA polymerase cannot start from nothing. It needs a primer, made of RNA by primase, to provide a free 3'-OH.

p: DNA strands have two different ends, called 5' and 3'. DNA polymerase can only attach a new nucleotide to the 3' end of an existing strand. So the new strand always grows from 5' toward 3'.
It also cannot start on its own. It needs a short RNA primer that gives it a 3'-OH to build on.

mem: New DNA is made 5' to 3'
Polymerase needs a primer with a free 3'-OH
Lagging strand makes Okazaki fragments
q7.trap: Mixing up the template direction (read 3' to 5') with the direction of new synthesis (5' to 3').
q7.plain: Building a train where you can only add cars to the back. You can never add to the front, and you need a first car already in place.

fig.cap: The leading strand is made continuously; the lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments, each primed, then joined by DNA ligase.

ox: Wrong. Helicase unwinds the double helix. That unwinding is what creates the positive supercoils ahead of the fork. Trap: helicase causes the problem; it does not fix it.
Correct. Topoisomerase cuts one or both DNA strands, lets the DNA swivel to release tension, and then reseals the cut. This relieves the supercoiling.
Wrong. Ligase seals nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone, such as between Okazaki fragments. It does not release twisting strain.
Wrong. Primase makes short RNA primers so that polymerase can start. It has no role in supercoiling.

p: When helicase unwinds a stretch of DNA, the DNA ahead gets overwound and tight. This is called positive supercoiling. If it builds up, replication stalls.
Topoisomerase solves this. It briefly cuts the DNA, lets it spin to relax, and reseals it. In bacteria, gyrase is a topoisomerase targeted by some antibiotics.

mem: Helicase unwinds
Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling by cutting and rejoining
Primase makes RNA primers; ligase seals nicks
q8.trap: Picking helicase because it is at the fork. It creates the strain; topoisomerase removes it.
q8.plain: If you pull two twisted rope strands apart, the rope ahead of you gets twisted tighter. Someone has to snip, untwist, and tie it back.

ox: Wrong. A silent mutation changes the codon but still codes for the same amino acid. UAG codes for no amino acid, so this is not silent.
Wrong. Missense means a different amino acid is inserted. Here no amino acid is inserted. UAG is a stop signal.
Correct. UAG is a stop codon. Changing UAC (Tyr) to UAG ends translation early, so the protein is truncated. That is a nonsense mutation.
Wrong. A frameshift comes from adding or removing bases (not in multiples of 3), shifting every codon after it. Here one base was swapped, so the frame is intact.

p: A codon is three RNA bases that code for one amino acid. A point mutation swaps one base. Silent: same amino acid. Missense: different amino acid. Nonsense: a stop codon appears.
The stop codons are UAA, UAG, and UGA. If one appears early, translation ends early and the protein is shorter, usually non-functional.

mem: Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA
Silent: same amino acid; missense: different; nonsense: stop
Frameshift needs an insertion or deletion not divisible by 3
q9.mn: Stop codons: 'U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away' for UAA, UAG, UGA.
q9.trap: Calling it missense because one amino acid is replaced. Here it is replaced by a stop signal, not another amino acid.
q9.plain: A sentence with a typo that makes a different word is missense. A typo that puts a period in the middle of the sentence is nonsense: the sentence stops early.

fig.cap: One base change can be silent (same amino acid), missense (different amino acid) or nonsense (early stop, truncated protein).

ox: Wrong. With no lactose, the repressor stays bound to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. High glucose also keeps cAMP low. Transcription is off.
Wrong. Lactose releases the repressor, but glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP is not activated. You get only low-level transcription. Trap: thinking lactose alone is enough.

Correct. Lactose becomes allolactose, which binds the repressor and releases it from the operator. Low glucose raises cAMP, which binds CAP and helps RNA polymerase bind. Both signals together give maximum transcription.
Wrong. With no lactose, the repressor stays on the operator. Low glucose would make CAP active, but the gene is still blocked.

p: The lac operon holds genes to digest lactose. It has two controls. A repressor protein blocks the gene unless lactose (as allolactose) is present. That is negative control.

CAP is an activator. It works only when cAMP is high, which happens when glucose is low. That is positive control. Bacteria prefer glucose, so they switch on lactose genes fully only when lactose is present and glucose is gone.

mem: Lactose present: repressor off the operator
Glucose low: cAMP high: CAP active
Max expression needs lactose present AND glucose absent
q10.trap: Stopping once the repressor is released. You also need CAP activation, which needs low glucose.
q10.plain: A light turns on only if two switches are both on: 'there is food I can use' and 'my favorite food is gone'.

fig.cap: Meiosis I separates homologs and halves the chromosome number; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
fig.alt: One homologous pair followed through meiosis I and II.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. Sister chromatids do split in anaphase II, but the cells were already haploid (n) after meiosis I, and they stay haploid. This step looks just like mitosis, which is why it's tempting.
Not quite. S phase copies the DNA, so each chromosome ends up with two identical sister chromatids. That doubles the amount of DNA, but there are still the same number of chromosomes.
Not quite. Crossing over in prophase I swaps matching pieces between homologs. It mixes alleles and adds variety, but every cell still has the same number of chromosomes.
Correct. In anaphase I, each homolog (still made of two chromatids) moves to the opposite pole from its partner. Each new cell gets only one chromosome from each pair, so 2n becomes n.

concept.t: What halves the chromosome number in meiosis
p: A diploid (2n) cell has two copies of each chromosome, called homologs, one from each parent. Meiosis I pulls the homologs into different cells. Afterward each cell has just one of each pair, so it's haploid (n). That's why meiosis I is called the 'reductional' division.

Meiosis II then separates the sister chromatids, the two identical copies that make up each chromosome. That's like mitosis, and it doesn't change the chromosome number. It's called the 'equational' division.

mem: Meiosis I is reductional: homologs separate, 2n becomes n
Meiosis II is equational: sister chromatids separate
Crossing over happens in prophase I
d_1C_1.trap: Picking sister chromatid separation because it's the 'separation' you know from mitosis.
d_1C_1.plain: Think of pairs of shoes, one left and one right. Meiosis I gives each of two kids one shoe from every pair, so each kid has half as many. Meiosis II only separates each shoe from its exact copy, which doesn't change how many kinds of shoes each kid has.

fig.cap: A meiosis I error makes all four products abnormal; a meiosis II error makes two abnormal and two normal.
fig.alt: Meiosis I and meiosis II nondisjunction with gamete chromosome counts.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. In meiosis I, both homologs of the pair go to the same pole. So one daughter cell has an extra chromosome and the other is missing one. Meiosis II splits each into two, so all four gametes are abnormal: two n+1 and two n−1. (Aneuploid means having the wrong number of chromosomes.)

Not quite. Two normal and two abnormal gametes (one n+1 and one n−1) is what you get from nondisjunction in meiosis II. There, meiosis I went fine, and only one of the two cells messes up its second split. Here the error is in meiosis I, which affects both cells.
Not quite. Four normal gametes would mean everything separated correctly. The question says one pair failed to separate, so some gametes must have the wrong number.
Not quite. This leaves out the n−1 gametes. If one cell got both homologs, the other cell got neither, so its gametes must be missing that chromosome. They can't be normal.

concept.t: Nondisjunction in meiosis I vs. meiosis II
p: Nondisjunction means chromosomes fail to separate. In meiosis I, homologous pairs should split apart. If one pair stays together, one cell gets both and the other gets none of that chromosome.

Meiosis II then splits the sister chromatids in each cell. Both cells were already wrong, so all four gametes are wrong: two with one extra (n+1) and two with one missing (n−1). A meiosis II error is milder: two normal gametes, one n+1 and one n−1.

mem: Meiosis I error: all 4 gametes abnormal (2 n+1, 2 n−1)
Meiosis II error: 2 normal, 1 n+1, 1 n−1
Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids
d_1C_3.trap: Mixing up meiosis I and II errors. A meiosis I error ruins all four gametes.
d_1C_3.plain: Two kids are supposed to each take home one twin. If one kid takes both twins, the other gets none, and splitting up later can't fix it.

fig.cap: Founder effect: a small founding group can carry an allele at a very different frequency from the source population.
fig.alt: Mainland population, 10 founders, and island descendants with a higher rare-allele frequency.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. A few birds start a new population, carrying only a small sample of the mainland gene pool. A rare allele can become common just by luck of who made the trip. That's the founder effect.

Not quite. Gene flow is the ongoing movement of alleles between populations as migrants keep coming and going and breeding. One colonization event isn't continued exchange. Birds moving makes this tempting, but the key here is that the new group is small and cut off.

Not quite. Directional selection needs the allele to give a survival or reproductive edge, so carriers leave more offspring. The question doesn't mention any advantage, so chance is the better explanation.

Not quite. A bottleneck is when an existing population suddenly crashes, often from a disaster, and the few survivors rebuild it in the same place. Here, a small group starts a new population in a new place. Both involve few individuals, which is why they're easy to confuse.

p: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies, and it's strongest in small groups. The founder effect is drift that happens when a few individuals leave and start a new population.

Those founders carry only part of the original gene pool. A rare allele might be missing entirely, or it might be overrepresented. Its frequency in the new population shifts by chance, not because it helps anyone survive.

mem: Founder effect: a new colony started by a few individuals
Bottleneck: an existing population shrinks suddenly, like after a disaster
Both are genetic drift: random, not adaptive
d_1C_8.mn: Founders Find a new home; a Bottleneck squeezes the old one.
d_1C_8.trap: Founder effect (new place, a few colonists) versus bottleneck (same place, population crash).
d_1C_8.plain: Grab a handful from a big jar of mixed candy, and your handful might have lots of a rare flavor just by luck.

fig.cap: Observed recombination frequency rises with map distance but levels off at 50%, the value for unlinked genes. It can never exceed one half.
fig.alt: Curve of observed recombination frequency against true map distance approaching 50%.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Haldane map function.

ox: Not quite. Completely linked genes never get separated, so they'd show 0% recombination. At 50 cM, recombination is at its maximum, the opposite end.

Correct. A recombination frequency of 50% gives equal numbers of parental and recombinant offspring, which is exactly what independent assortment gives. So genes 50 cM or more apart behave as if unlinked.

Not quite. Recombination frequency can't go above 50%. An even number of crossovers between two genes puts the alleles back the way they started, so those offspring look parental. That caps what you can measure at 50%.
Not quite. No crossovers between the genes would mean complete linkage and 0% recombination. Genes 50 cM apart have crossovers between them very often.

p: Genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together because they're physically connected. Crossing over can break them apart. A centimorgan (cM) is a unit of distance: 1 cM is about 1% recombination.

If two genes are far enough apart, crossovers between them are so common that half the offspring are recombinant and half are parental. That's exactly the result independent assortment gives, so 50% is the maximum and means the genes act unlinked.

mem: 1 cM is about 1% recombination
Maximum recombination frequency is 50%
50% means they act unlinked
Closer genes, lower recombination
d_1C_11.trap: Thinking recombination can reach 100%, or that 50 cM means tightly linked.
d_1C_11.plain: Far-apart genes act like two separate coin flips: how one lands tells you nothing about the other.

fig.cap: Penetrance: does the genotype show at all? Expressivity: how strongly it shows in those affected.
fig.alt: Two rows of carriers showing variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

r: Does the carrier show the trait at all?

ox: Not quite. Variable expressivity means people who all show the trait have different severity, mild in one and severe in another. The first person shows no signs at all. That's a question of whether, not how much.
Not quite. Codominance means both alleles of a gene are fully expressed in a heterozygote, like AB blood type. It doesn't explain why someone has no phenotype.
Not quite. Epistasis is when one gene hides the effect of a different gene, like a gene that blocks pigment hiding a coat-color gene. The question doesn't describe any second gene.
Correct. Penetrance is the percent of people with a genotype who show any phenotype. A person who carries the allele but shows no signs is an example of incomplete (reduced) penetrance.

p: Penetrance asks: does the person show the trait at all? If only 80% of people with an allele show signs, penetrance is 80%. Anything under 100% is incomplete penetrance.
Expressivity asks: among the people who show the trait, how strong is it? When one person has mild disease and another has severe disease from the same allele, that's variable expressivity.

mem: Penetrance: does the trait show up at all (yes or no)
Expressivity: how severe it is when it does
Incomplete penetrance: a carrier with no phenotype
d_1C_15.trap: Mixing up penetrance (whether) with expressivity (how much).
d_1C_15.plain: Penetrance is whether the light turns on. Expressivity is how bright it shines.

ox: Wrong. Hexokinase is the first step and traps glucose in the cell as G6P, but G6P can still go to glycogen or the pentose phosphate pathway. It is not the committed step.
Correct. PFK-1 turns fructose-6-phosphate into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. After this step the sugar is committed to glycolysis. It is slowed by ATP and sped up by AMP and F2,6BP.
Wrong. Pyruvate kinase is regulated, but it is the last step, after the commitment has already been made.
Wrong. This enzyme starts the pentose phosphate pathway, a different route. Do not confuse it with glycolysis.

p: Glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvate. The committed step is the one after which the molecule has no other option but to continue down the pathway. It is usually also the slowest, regulated step.
In glycolysis this is PFK-1. ATP signals the cell has enough energy and turns it down. AMP signals low energy and turns it up.

mem: PFK-1: F6P to F1,6BP is the committed, rate-limiting step.
ATP and citrate inhibit PFK-1; AMP and F2,6BP activate it.
Hexokinase = first step; pyruvate kinase = last step.
q14.trap: Choosing hexokinase because it is first. First is not the same as committed.
q14.plain: Think of a one-way toll gate on a highway. Once your car goes through, you cannot take any exit but the one ahead.

fig.cap: Glycolysis spends ATP at hexokinase and PFK-1 (the committed step) and makes ATP at two substrate-level steps, for a net 2 ATP per glucose.
fig.alt: Glycolysis from glucose to 2 pyruvate with the ATP-using and ATP-making enzymes labeled.

ox: Correct. Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but spends 2 early on, so the net is 2 ATP. It also makes 2 NADH.
Wrong. 4 ATP is the gross yield. You must subtract the 2 ATP invested in the first steps.
Wrong. About 30-32 ATP is the total from complete aerobic breakdown (glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, TCA cycle, electron transport chain).
Wrong. Glycolysis makes NADH. FADH₂ is made in the TCA cycle and in fatty acid oxidation.

p: Glycolysis splits one glucose into two pyruvate. Early steps spend 2 ATP to prepare the sugar. Later steps make 4 ATP.
Net means what is left after paying the cost. It also makes 2 NADH, an electron carrier that can later be used to make more ATP.

mem: Glycolysis net: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate.
Gross ATP = 4; invested = 2.
Aerobic total is about 30-32 ATP.

fm.f: Net ATP = ATP made - ATP spent
fm.why: Net yield means profit after the investment.

q15.trap: Reporting the gross 4 ATP instead of the net 2 ATP.
q15.plain: You pay 2 dollars to enter a game and win 4 dollars. You walked away with 2 dollars of profit.

fig.cap: Glycolysis spends ATP at hexokinase and PFK-1 (the committed step) and makes ATP at two substrate-level steps, for a net 2 ATP per glucose.
fig.alt: Glycolysis from glucose to 2 pyruvate with the ATP-using and ATP-making enzymes labeled.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Wrong. Complex I is blocked by rotenone, not cyanide.
Correct. Cyanide binds the iron in complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), so electrons cannot pass to O₂. The whole chain backs up and O₂ use stops.
Wrong. ATP synthase is blocked by oligomycin. That would stop ATP making but the chain problem is different.
Wrong. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is inhibited by malonate, not cyanide.

p: The electron transport chain is a line of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons are passed down the line and finally given to oxygen at complex IV, forming water.
If complex IV is blocked, electrons cannot leave the chain. Everything upstream backs up and oxygen is no longer used.

mem: Cyanide (and CO, azide) block complex IV.
Rotenone blocks complex I; malonate blocks complex II.
Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase.
q16.trap: Mixing up which poison blocks which complex. Oxygen is the final acceptor, so the O₂-related poison hits complex IV.
q16.plain: It is like a bucket line passing water to the end person. If the last person is stuck, the whole line stops.

fig.cap: Electrons enter from NADH and succinate and leave at Complex IV, where O₂ is reduced to water. Cyanide blocks Complex IV.
fig.alt: Electron transport chain with Complexes I to IV, coenzyme Q and cytochrome c; O₂ reduced to water at Complex IV.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. A proton leak is an uncoupler. The gradient cannot build, so the chain runs faster to try to fix it and uses more O₂. ATP synthase has little gradient to use, so ATP falls. The energy is lost as heat.
Wrong. Falling O₂ use fits an electron transport chain inhibitor such as cyanide. A leak makes the chain work harder, not slower.
Wrong. ATP synthesis needs the proton gradient. If protons leak back, there is less drive to make ATP.
Wrong. Glycolysis makes only 2 net ATP and cannot make up the loss. Also, the ETC and gradient are directly affected.

p: The electron transport chain pumps protons out of the matrix to build a gradient. Protons flow back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. This links (couples) O₂ use to ATP making.
An uncoupler lets protons leak back in without passing through ATP synthase. The chain speeds up, O₂ use rises, ATP falls, and the extra energy becomes heat.

mem: Uncoupler: O₂ use up, ATP down, heat up.
Examples: DNP, thermogenin (UCP1) in brown fat.
Inhibitors of the ETC lower O₂ use.
q17.trap: Thinking less ATP always means less O₂ use. Uncouplers speed up O₂ use.
q17.plain: Picture a water wheel with a hole in the pool above. The pump works nonstop to refill the pool, but the wheel barely turns.

fig.cap: Respiratory control: ADP speeds O₂ use, oligomycin slows it by blocking ATP synthase, and an uncoupler (DNP) speeds it again without making ATP.
fig.alt: Oxygen-electrode trace: O₂ falls slowly, faster after ADP, slowly after oligomycin, fast after DNP.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code; values illustrative.

ox: Wrong. CoA attaches to the fatty acid in the cytosol but the acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner membrane by itself.
Correct. Carnitine swaps places with CoA, carries the acyl group across, and CoA is reattached in the matrix, where β-oxidation occurs.
Wrong. Albumin carries free fatty acids through the blood, not across the mitochondrial membrane.
Wrong. Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the gut through lymph and blood.

p: β-oxidation, the breakdown of fatty acids for energy, happens inside the mitochondrial matrix. Long fatty acids must get past the inner mitochondrial membrane, which blocks them.
Carnitine acts as a ferry. It picks up the acyl group, carries it across, and drops it off inside the matrix.

mem: Carnitine carries long-chain acyl groups into the matrix.
CPT-I is the rate-limiting step; malonyl-CoA inhibits it.
Albumin = blood transport; chylomicron = dietary fat transport.
q18.trap: Picking CoA because it is attached to the fatty acid. It activates it but cannot cross.
q18.plain: Carnitine is like a ferry that carries cars across a river where no bridge exists.

fig.cap: Long-chain fatty acids need the carnitine shuttle (CPT-I, translocase, CPT-II) to reach the matrix; short- and medium-chain fatty acids cross without carnitine.
fig.alt: Mitochondrial membranes with long-chain fatty acids blocked without carnitine and medium-chain fatty acids crossing freely.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: A cis double bond kinks the tail, so lipids pack loosely and the membrane stays fluid; saturated and trans tails pack tightly.
fig.alt: Stearic, oleic and elaidic acid chains compared for packing.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: Gap junctions (connexons) join the cytoplasm of neighboring cells so ions and small dyes can pass; the other junctions seal or anchor.
fig.alt: Two epithelial cells with tight, adherens, desmosome, gap junction and hemidesmosome labeled.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: SGLT1 uses the Na⁺ gradient made by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Ouabain stops the pump, the gradient runs down, and glucose uptake falls.
fig.alt: Intestinal cell with apical SGLT1, basolateral GLUT2 and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. SGLT pulls glucose in using the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. With the pump blocked, the gradient fades and glucose uptake falls.
Not quite. Blocking the pump lets Na⁺ build up inside the cell. What SGLT needs isn't Na⁺ itself but a big difference between outside and inside. That difference shrinks, so SGLT slows down.
Not quite. SGLT doesn't use ATP directly. It's secondary active transport, running on the Na⁺ gradient that the ATP-using pump built. Block the pump and SGLT feels it.

Not quite. SGLT moves glucose in only when Na⁺ flows in alongside it. Once the Na⁺ gradient fades, the transporter loses its driving force and glucose uptake slows. The expected change is less glucose coming in, not glucose flowing backward.

p: Primary active transport uses ATP directly. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the classic example: it pumps Na⁺ out of the cell, keeping Na⁺ low inside.

Secondary active transport uses that stored gradient instead of ATP. SGLT lets Na⁺ flow in, and glucose comes along for the ride. If the pump is blocked, the gradient runs down and glucose uptake goes with it.

mem: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase = primary active transport; it builds the gradient
SGLT = secondary active; carries Na⁺ and glucose in together
Ouabain and digoxin block the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
d_2A_3.trap: Thinking a cotransporter uses ATP itself. It runs on the gradient an ATP pump made.
d_2A_3.plain: A water slide only works if someone keeps hauling water to the top. Stop the hauling, and the slide dries up.

fig.cap: Secreted proteins go rough ER → cis Golgi → medial → trans Golgi → vesicles to the cell surface.
fig.alt: ER, Golgi cisternae from cis to trans, and the three exit routes.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. The protein is made on the rough ER, sent to the Golgi for processing, packed into secretory vesicles, and released by exocytosis at the plasma membrane.

Not quite. This puts the Golgi before the rough ER, which is backwards: proteins start in the ER and then go to the Golgi. Also, lysosomes are digestion compartments, not a stop on the way out of the cell.
Not quite. The nucleus holds the DNA and makes the mRNA, but proteins are built on ribosomes outside it. And this route ends in a lysosome, not at the cell surface where secretion happens.
Not quite. The smooth ER has no ribosomes; it makes lipids and handles detox. Peroxisomes carry out oxidation reactions. Neither is part of the path a secreted protein takes.

p: Proteins meant for export are built by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER), which is studded with ribosomes. They're fed into the ER's inner space as they're made.

Vesicles (small membrane bubbles) carry them to the Golgi, which modifies and sorts them. Secretory vesicles then fuse with the plasma membrane and release the proteins outside, which is called exocytosis.

mem: Order: rough ER, Golgi, vesicle, plasma membrane
Rough ER makes secreted and membrane proteins
Lysosomes are a different destination from secretion
d_2A_10.trap: Putting the Golgi before the ER, or sending a secreted protein to a lysosome.
d_2A_10.plain: It's a factory line: build the product, wrap and label it, load it on a truck, and drive it out the front gate.

fig.cap: Simple squamous epithelium is one flat layer, giving the thinnest barrier and the fastest diffusion (Fick's law).
fig.alt: Alveolar simple squamous barrier compared with a thick stratified layer.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. Stratified squamous has many layers stacked up, like skin. It's built to protect, and gases would diffuse through it far too slowly.
Not quite. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines the larger airways, where its cilia sweep mucus up and out. It's too thick for gas exchange.
Correct. One thin layer of flat cells gives the shortest possible distance, so oxygen and carbon dioxide pass quickly between air and blood.
Not quite. Columnar cells are tall, built for absorbing and secreting, like in the gut lining. That extra height makes the diffusion distance longer.

p: Epithelium is tissue that covers surfaces. 'Simple' means one layer; 'stratified' means many layers. 'Squamous' means flat; 'columnar' means tall; 'cuboidal' means cube-shaped.
Gas moves by diffusion, which is faster over a short distance. A single layer of flat cells is the thinnest option, so it's what lines the alveoli and the capillary walls.

mem: Simple squamous: diffusion (alveoli, capillaries)
Stratified squamous: protection (skin)
Simple columnar: absorption (gut); pseudostratified ciliated: airways
d_2A_17.trap: Picking the tough, protective epithelium. Exchange needs thin, not tough.
d_2A_17.plain: Passing a note through a thin sheet of paper is easy. Passing it through a thick book is not.

fig.cap: A section of plasma membrane: integral and peripheral proteins sit in a fluid bilayer where lateral diffusion is fast and flip-flop is slow. Below, the current model is compared with the abandoned protein-sandwich model.
fig.alt: Schematic bilayer of phospholipids with a single-pass and a multipass integral protein, a glycan, and a peripheral protein on the cytosolic face; a green double arrow labeled lateral diffusion fast; a red arrow across the bilayer labeled flip-flop slow. Lower panels contrast the fluid mosaic model with the Davson-Danielli protein-lipid-protein sandwich.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. This is the older Davson–Danielli model, which pictured protein sheets coating both sides of a lipid layer. Freeze-fracture images later showed proteins sitting inside the bilayer, poking through it, so the sandwich idea was dropped.

Not quite. Flipping between leaflets is slow, because the lipid's polar head would have to pass through the oily core. It needs flippase enzymes to happen quickly. The fast motion is sideways, within one leaflet.
Not quite. The bilayer is fluid, not a rigid grid. Experiments like FRAP, where a bleached spot on the membrane quickly fills back in with glowing proteins, show that many proteins drift sideways.
Correct. The membrane is a two-dimensional fluid. Lipids and many proteins slide sideways within their own leaflet, and the proteins are scattered through it like a mosaic.

p: A plasma membrane is a bilayer: two layers of phospholipids with their water-loving heads facing out toward the water and their oily tails tucked inside. Proteins are embedded in it or attached to its surface.
'Fluid' means the parts can slide around sideways. 'Mosaic' means proteins are scattered through it like tiles. Moving from one layer to the other is rare and slow unless an enzyme helps.

mem: Sideways movement is fast; flip-flop is slow without flippase
Proteins are integral (embedded) or peripheral (attached to the surface)
Fluid mosaic replaced the protein-sandwich model
x2A_001.trap: Thinking lipids flip easily between leaflets, or that proteins are locked in place.
x2A_001.plain: Think of a crowded dance floor: people slide around freely, but nobody can easily jump up to the floor above.

fig.cap: Illustrative model curves of fluidity versus temperature. Without cholesterol the bilayer melts sharply from gel to fluid; with cholesterol the change is gentler, so the membrane is more fluid in the cold and less fluid when warm.
fig.alt: Graph of membrane fluidity versus temperature from 0 to 50 degrees Celsius. A blue curve without cholesterol rises steeply around 25 degrees from low to high fluidity. An orange curve with cholesterol rises gradually, sitting above the blue curve in the cold region and below it in the warm region.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph from illustrative logistic curves; it shows the well-established qualitative effect, not measured data.

ox: Not quite. Making the membrane stiffer is what cholesterol does at high temperature, where it holds back the tails' motion. In the cold, it does the opposite and keeps the membrane fluid.
Not quite. Cholesterol fills gaps between lipids, which makes it harder for ions and small polar molecules to sneak through. So it lowers permeability, not raises it.
Not quite. Cholesterol isn't an enzyme, so it can't speed up any reaction. Lipid flip-flop is sped up by enzymes called flippases.
Correct. Cholesterol's rigid ring wedges between the fatty acid tails so they can't pack tightly into a gel. That keeps the membrane fluid in the cold.

p: Membrane fluidity changes with temperature. In the cold, lipid tails pack tightly and the membrane stiffens. In the heat, the tails move more and the membrane gets loose and leaky.
Cholesterol sits between the tails and pushes back against both extremes. In the cold, it blocks tight packing, so fluidity goes up. In the heat, it limits tail motion, so fluidity goes down.

mem: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer
Cold: blocks packing, so more fluid. Hot: holds tails back, so less fluid
Unsaturated tails raise fluidity; long, saturated tails lower it
x2A_002.trap: Saying cholesterol always makes membranes stiffer. Its effect depends on temperature.
x2A_002.plain: Cholesterol is like a few pencils slipped into a stack of papers. In the cold, they stop the papers from stacking flat and stiff. When things get shaky, they keep the papers from sliding all over.

fig.cap: Gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane outside a thin peptidoglycan layer, an extra barrier that keeps many large or hydrophobic agents out. Gram-positives have a thick wall and no outer membrane.
fig.alt: Gram-positive and Gram-negative cell envelopes side by side.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: Wall-synthesis inhibitors such as penicillin kill only cells that are building new wall, so growing cells lyse and non-growing cells survive.
fig.alt: Viable count over time with penicillin added in exponential versus stationary phase.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Illustrative.

fig.cap: A batch culture shows lag (cells adjust, little division), exponential growth, stationary phase (nutrient limits growth) and death.
fig.alt: Log viable count against time with lag, exponential, stationary and death phases.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Illustrative model.

fig.cap: Oxygen diffuses only about 0.1 to 0.2 mm, so a tumor beyond 1 to 2 mm stalls (with death balancing division) until VEGF recruits new vessels.
fig.alt: Tumor with a hypoxic core secreting VEGF, new vessel sprouts, and an anti-VEGF antibody.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall on the outside and no outer membrane. The thick wall traps the crystal violet dye, so they stain purple.
Wrong. This is Gram-negative bacteria, which have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane holding LPS (lipopolysaccharide). Trap: mixing up the two groups.
Wrong. Almost all bacteria have a wall. Mycoplasma is the famous exception. Trap: choosing the exception instead of the rule.
Wrong. Gram-negative cells stain pink or red because the thin wall loses the purple dye. Trap: remembering pink and linking it to the wrong group.

p: The Gram stain sorts bacteria by their cell wall. Peptidoglycan is a mesh of sugars and amino acids that gives the wall strength.
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, no outer membrane, stains purple. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan, plus an outer membrane with LPS, stains pink.

mem: Gram-positive = thick wall, purple, no outer membrane.
Gram-negative = thin wall, pink, outer membrane with LPS.
Mycoplasma has no cell wall.
q23.trap: Swapping the colors. Positive keeps the purple stain; negative loses it and shows pink.
q23.plain: A thick winter coat holds the dye in like a sponge. A thin jacket lets it wash out.

ox: Wrong. Transformation is when a bacterium picks up free, naked DNA from its surroundings. No virus is involved. Trap: both move DNA, so they sound alike.
Correct. In transduction, a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) carries bacterial DNA from one cell to another. The virus is the vector.
Wrong. Conjugation moves DNA directly between two bacteria through a sex pilus (a tube-like bridge). No virus needed.
Wrong. Binary fission is how a bacterium divides into two copies. It does not transfer DNA between different cells.

p: Bacteria share genes in three ways. Each has a different carrier.
Transformation: free DNA from the environment. Transduction: a bacteriophage carries the DNA. Conjugation: a direct bridge (sex pilus) between two cells.

mem: Transformation = naked DNA taken up.
Transduction = virus (phage) carries DNA.
Conjugation = pilus contact between cells.
Binary fission = reproduction, not gene transfer.
q24.mn: Transduction has the word 'duct' like a delivery tube: a virus delivers the DNA.
q24.trap: Mixing up transformation and transduction. Look for the word 'bacteriophage' or 'virus' to pick transduction.
q24.plain: Transduction is like a mail carrier (the virus) delivering a package (DNA) from one house to another.

ox: Correct. Reverse transcriptase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase. It reads the viral RNA and builds a DNA copy.
Wrong. Integrase inserts the finished DNA copy into the host genome. It comes after the copy is made. Trap: both enzymes are retrovirus steps.
Wrong. RNA replicase copies RNA into RNA, which is used by some other RNA viruses. A retrovirus needs RNA to DNA.
Wrong. DNA polymerase I in bacteria removes RNA primers and fills gaps. It reads a DNA template, not an RNA genome.

p: A retrovirus (like HIV) stores its genes as RNA. The host cell reads DNA, so the virus needs to convert its RNA to DNA first.
Reverse transcriptase does this conversion. Then integrase puts the DNA into the host chromosome, where it is copied as a normal gene.

mem: Reverse transcriptase: RNA to DNA.
Integrase: inserts viral DNA into the host genome.
Retroviruses go RNA to DNA to RNA to protein.
q25.trap: Choosing integrase. It joins DNA into the genome but does not make the DNA from RNA.
q25.plain: It is like translating a message from a foreign language into the language the town speaks, so the locals can use it.

fig.cap: DNA damage stabilizes p53, which turns on p21. p21 blocks the cyclin–CDKs that phosphorylate Rb, so E2F stays bound and the cell pauses in G1.
fig.alt: Pathway from DNA damage through p53 and p21 to blocked cyclin–CDK and Rb–E2F.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: p53 is kept low by constant destruction; DNA damage stabilizes it. It then arrests the cycle (p21) or triggers apoptosis (Bax, PUMA). Cells without p53 keep dividing with damage.
fig.alt: Flowchart from DNA damage to p53 and its two outcomes.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: p53 is kept low by constant destruction; DNA damage stabilizes it. It then arrests the cycle (p21) or triggers apoptosis (Bax, PUMA). Cells without p53 keep dividing with damage.
fig.alt: Flowchart from DNA damage to p53 and its two outcomes.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: An unattached kinetochore keeps the spindle checkpoint on: APC/C stays inhibited, cohesin is not cut, and the cell is held in mitosis.
fig.alt: Spindle assembly checkpoint from an unattached kinetochore to cohesin cleavage.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: Apoptosis is orderly: the cell shrinks into membrane-wrapped bodies that are engulfed without spilling contents. Necrosis swells and bursts, causing inflammation.
fig.alt: Apoptosis and necrosis compared step by step.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. p53 is a tumor suppressor. After DNA damage it stops the cell at the G1/S checkpoint so repair can happen. If damage is too bad, it triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death).
Wrong. Oncogenes push the cell to divide. p53 does the opposite. Trap: confusing tumor suppressors with oncogenes.
Wrong. Cyclins rise and fall with the cell cycle. p53 is a transcription factor that turns genes on or off, not a cyclin.
Wrong. Telomerase lengthens telomeres (chromosome ends). It is not related to p53's role.

concept.t: p53, the guardian of the genome
p: p53 is a protein that checks for DNA damage. It is a tumor suppressor: a gene whose job is to stop uncontrolled growth.
When DNA is damaged, p53 turns on genes (like p21) that pause the cycle at G1/S. If repair fails, p53 pushes the cell into apoptosis.

mem: p53 = tumor suppressor; loss of p53 helps cancer grow.
It arrests the cell at G1/S or triggers apoptosis.
Oncogenes speed division; tumor suppressors brake it.
q26.trap: Calling p53 an oncogene. Loss of a tumor suppressor causes cancer; gain of an oncogene does.
q26.plain: p53 is a safety inspector who stops the factory line when something is broken, and shuts down the machine if it cannot be fixed.

ox: Correct. Ectoderm is the outer germ layer. It forms the epidermis (skin) and the nervous system.
Wrong. Heart and kidneys come from mesoderm, the middle layer. Trap: thinking of organs in general as outer structures.
Wrong. Gut lining and lungs come from endoderm, the inner layer.
Wrong. Bone and skeletal muscle come from mesoderm.

p: Early embryos have three layers of cells. Each becomes different body parts.
Ectoderm (outer): skin and nervous system. Mesoderm (middle): muscle, bone, heart, kidneys, blood. Endoderm (inner): gut lining, lungs, liver, pancreas.

mem: Ectoderm = skin (epidermis) + nervous system.
Mesoderm = muscle, bone, heart, kidney, blood.
Endoderm = gut lining, lungs, liver, pancreas.
q27.trap: Mixing up mesoderm and endoderm for organs such as kidneys and lungs.
q27.sc: Ecto = outer, like exterior: the outer layer makes the outer covering (skin) and the nervous system. Endo = inner, like the gut lining.
q27.plain: Think of a three-layer cake. The top layer becomes the skin and the brain, the middle becomes muscles and bones, the bottom becomes the insides of tubes like the gut.

ox: Wrong. In prophase, chromatin condenses into chromosomes and the spindle begins to form. The chromatids are still joined.
Wrong. In metaphase, chromosomes line up at the middle plate. They are still paired. Trap: this is just before the separation.
Correct. In anaphase, cohesin (the protein glue holding sister chromatids) is cleaved. The chromatids are pulled to opposite poles.
Wrong. In telophase, nuclear envelopes re-form around the separated sets. Separation already happened.

p: A sister chromatid is one of two identical copies of a chromosome, joined at the centromere. Mitosis splits them so each new cell gets one copy.
The order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Splitting happens in anaphase.

mem: Prophase: condense. Metaphase: line up. Anaphase: apart. Telophase: two nuclei.
Anaphase = sister chromatids separate (mitosis).
In meiosis I, homologs separate; in meiosis II, sister chromatids separate.
q28.mn: PMAT: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase. 'A' for Apart.
q28.trap: Picking metaphase because it is the famous lineup stage. Separation comes right after it.
q28.plain: Two kids holding hands line up in the middle of the room (metaphase). In anaphase someone lets go and each kid walks to opposite sides.

ox: Correct. High CO₂, high H⁺ (lower pH) in active muscle lowers Hb's affinity for O₂ (Bohr effect), so the curve shifts right and more O₂ is released.
Wrong. Cooler temperature increases affinity and shifts the curve left. Trap: forgetting heat shifts right.
Wrong. Fetal Hb binds O₂ more tightly than adult Hb, shifting the curve left so it can take O₂ from mom. Trap: thinking fetal Hb unloads easily.
Wrong. CO binds Hb strongly and also makes remaining O₂ bind more tightly, shifting left. Trap: assuming a poison lowers affinity.

p: The oxyhemoglobin curve shows how full Hb is with O₂ at different O₂ pressures. A right shift means Hb lets go of O₂ more easily (lower affinity). A left shift means Hb holds O₂ tighter.
Right shift: more CO₂, more H⁺ (lower pH), higher temperature, more 2,3-BPG. These happen in working muscle, which needs more O₂.

mem: Right shift: high CO₂, H⁺, temperature, 2,3-BPG
Left shift: opposites, plus fetal Hb and CO
Right shift = lower affinity = more unloading
q34.mn: CADET face Right: CO₂, Acid, 2,3-BPG (DPG), Exercise, Temperature all shift the curve right.
q34.trap: Mixing up which direction means higher affinity. Right = release.
q34.plain: Hot, busy muscles call out for oxygen, so the delivery truck drops off its cargo more easily.

ox: Correct. Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to keep Na⁺ and excrete K⁺. Water follows Na⁺, raising blood volume.
Wrong. Inserting aquaporins to reabsorb water is ADH. Trap: mixing up the two hormones.
Wrong. Decreasing Na⁺ reabsorption is ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide). Aldosterone does the opposite. Trap: reversing the direction.
Wrong. Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, mostly by transporters, not by aldosterone. Trap: picking the wrong segment.

p: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex. It acts in the distal tubule and collecting duct. It makes cells reabsorb sodium (Na⁺) and secrete potassium (K⁺).
Water follows sodium by osmosis, so blood volume and pressure rise. The renin-angiotensin system triggers aldosterone release when pressure is low.

mem: Aldosterone: Na⁺ in, K⁺ out, water follows
ADH: water only, via aquaporins
ANP: opposite of aldosterone
q35.plain: Aldosterone is a salt-saver. It tells the kidney to keep salt and water in the body.

ox: Wrong. Pepsin is the stomach protease, made from pepsinogen. It does not activate trypsinogen. Trap: choosing the most famous protease.
Correct. Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal lining cuts trypsinogen into active trypsin. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic zymogens.
Wrong. HCl activates pepsinogen to pepsin in the stomach, not trypsinogen. Trap: mixing up the two activations.
Wrong. Bile salts emulsify fats, breaking large drops into small ones. They do not cut proteins. Trap: confusing digestive helpers.

p: Pancreatic enzymes are made as inactive precursors called zymogens, so they do not digest the pancreas itself. Trypsinogen is one.
In the duodenum (first part of the small intestine), enteropeptidase cuts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and other zymogens (chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase).

mem: Enteropeptidase: trypsinogen to trypsin
Trypsin activates the other zymogens
HCl activates pepsinogen in the stomach
q36.trap: Choosing pepsin or HCl because they are the stomach's famous activators.
q36.plain: A safety cap keeps a tool locked. A key in the intestine unlocks the first tool, and that tool unlocks the rest.

ox: Wrong. Helper T cells release cytokines that direct B cells and others, but they do not make antibodies. Trap: confusing coordinating with producing.
Correct. Plasma cells are activated B cells that make and secrete large amounts of antibodies.
Wrong. Macrophages eat pathogens and show antigens to T cells. They do not secrete antibodies. Trap: assuming all immune cells do all jobs.
Wrong. NK cells kill infected or tumor cells directly, without antibodies. Trap: mixing innate and adaptive cells.

p: B cells are white blood cells of the adaptive immune system. When a B cell meets its antigen (a molecule it recognizes), often with help from helper T cells, it becomes a plasma cell.
Plasma cells are antibody factories. Antibodies are proteins that bind specific antigens. Some B cells become memory B cells for future infections.

mem: Plasma cell = secreting B cell
Helper T (CD4) = coordinate
Cytotoxic T (CD8) and NK = kill cells directly
q37.trap: Picking helper T cells because they are called the 'conductors' of the response.
q37.plain: A B cell is a recruit who learns the enemy's face. A plasma cell is the factory that mass-produces wanted posters for that face.

ox: Wrong. The stomach mostly churns and starts digesting protein. Only alcohol and a few drugs cross its wall well. Trap: thinking digestion and absorption happen in the same place.
Correct. The small intestine is lined with folds, villi and tiny microvilli, which create a huge surface area. Sugars, amino acids, fats, vitamins and minerals are absorbed here.
Wrong. The large intestine mainly takes back water and electrolytes and holds waste. Trap: picking the 'last stop' because it feels like the final step.
Wrong. The esophagus is only a tube that moves food by peristalsis (wave-like squeezing). Nothing is absorbed there.

p: Digestion means breaking food into small pieces. Absorption means moving those pieces into the blood or lymph. Most absorption happens in the small intestine.
Its wall has villi (finger-like folds) covered in microvilli (tiny hairs on each cell). These make a very large surface area, so nutrients pass into the body quickly.

mem: Small intestine = main site of nutrient absorption
Villi and microvilli = more surface area
Large intestine = water and electrolytes
Stomach absorbs almost nothing (alcohol, some drugs)
q38.trap: Do not confuse where digestion starts (mouth, stomach) with where absorption mostly happens (small intestine).
q38.plain: A paper towel with lots of folds soaks up more water than a flat sheet. The villi are the folds.

fig.cap: The biceps inserts close to the elbow, so it must pull far harder than the load to balance the torque.
fig.alt: Forearm lever with biceps, forearm weight and a 2 kg load at their distances.

ox: Correct. Average velocity = displacement ÷ time. After one full lap she's back at the start, so displacement = 0 m, and 0 ÷ 80 s = 0 m/s.
Not quite. 5 m/s is her average speed: 400 m ÷ 80 s. Speed uses total distance, but velocity uses displacement, which is zero for a full lap. The two are easy to mix up.
Not quite. 10 m/s would mean 400 m in 40 s, or doubling the average speed. Nothing in the question supports either. It's a guess built from the numbers given.
Not quite. 400 is the distance in meters, not a velocity. It never gets divided by the time, so the units don't even match m/s.

p: Distance is the total length of the path you travel. Displacement is the straight-line change in position, from start to finish, including which way. A full lap has a distance of 400 m but a displacement of 0 m.
Average speed = distance ÷ time. Average velocity = displacement ÷ time. So if you end where you started, your average velocity is zero, no matter how fast you ran.

mem: Average velocity = displacement ÷ time
Average speed = distance ÷ time
Round trip: displacement = 0

fm.f: v_avg = Δx / t, where v_avg = average velocity, Δx = displacement (end position − start position), t = time
fm.v: Δx = 0 m (back at the start); t = 80 s; v_avg = ?
fm.why: Velocity is defined using displacement, not distance traveled.
fm.nc: Zero divided by any number is zero.

steps: Write the formula: v_avg = Δx ÷ t.
Write down the values: she ends where she started, so Δx = 0 m; t = 80 s.
Plug in: v_avg = 0 m ÷ 80 s = 0 m/s.
d_4A_1.trap: Picking 5 m/s, which is average speed. The question asks for average velocity.
d_4A_1.plain: Walk all the way around the block and end at your front door. You walked a lot, but you're no farther from home than when you started.

fig.cap: A horizontally thrown ball keeps vₓ while gravity adds v_y = gt; add the parts as vectors to get the speed.
fig.alt: Ball leaving a cliff with velocity components at 0, 1 and 2 s.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. 10 m/s is only the sideways speed, which doesn't change. But gravity has been speeding the ball up downward for 2 s, so the total speed is bigger.
Not quite. 20 m/s is only the downward speed after 2 s (10 × 2). The ball is still moving sideways at 10 m/s too, so the total speed is more than 20 m/s.
Correct. Sideways speed stays 10 m/s. Downward speed = gt = 10 × 2 = 20 m/s. Combine at right angles: √(10² + 20²) = √(100 + 400) = √500 ≈ 22 m/s.
Not quite. 30 m/s comes from 10 + 20. That would be right only if both speeds pointed the same way. They're at right angles, so you need √(10² + 20²) ≈ 22 m/s.

p: A projectile's sideways motion and its up-and-down motion don't affect each other. With no air resistance, nothing pushes the ball sideways, so its sideways speed stays the same. Meanwhile gravity speeds it up downward by g = 10 m/s every second.
A ball thrown horizontally starts with zero downward speed, so after t seconds its downward speed is just gt.

Its actual speed is the length of the diagonal made by the two parts. They're at right angles, so use the Pythagorean theorem: v = √(vₓ² + v_y²). The answer is always bigger than either part, but smaller than their sum.

mem: Sideways speed stays constant
Downward speed = gt (thrown horizontally)
Combine with v = √(vₓ² + v_y²)

fm.f: v = √(vₓ² + v_y²), where v = total speed, vₓ = sideways speed, v_y = downward speed = gt
fm.why: The two parts are at right angles, so they form the two short sides of a right triangle.

steps: Write the formula: v = √(vₓ² + v_y²), with v_y = gt.
Write down the values: vₓ = 10 m/s, g = 10 m/s², t = 2.0 s.
Find the downward speed: v_y = 10 × 2 = 20 m/s.
Square each part: 10² = 100 and 20² = 400.
Take the square root: √500 ≈ 22 m/s.
d_4A_3.sc: The answer has to be more than 20 (the bigger part) and less than 30 (10 + 20). Only 22 fits.
d_4A_3.trap: Adding the two speeds straight to get 30 m/s.
d_4A_3.plain: A ball rolling off a table keeps moving sideways at the same pace, while it falls faster and faster. Its real speed combines both.

fig.cap: Momentum is conserved in every collision; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones. With no outside force, the center of mass keeps its velocity.
fig.alt: Table of collision types and a momentum vector sum for two sticking pucks.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. Both at v/2 does keep momentum: m × v/2 + m × v/2 = mv. But kinetic energy drops: 2 × ½m(v/2)² = ¼mv², only half of the starting ½mv². An elastic collision can't lose kinetic energy.

Correct. For equal masses in a head-on elastic collision, the only result that keeps both momentum and kinetic energy is a swap. The first ball stops, and the second leaves at the first ball's original speed.
Not quite. Sticking together is a perfectly inelastic collision, which loses the most kinetic energy possible. The question says the collision is elastic.
Not quite. If the first ball bounced back at speed v and the second went forward at v, the total momentum would be −mv + mv = 0. It started at mv, so momentum wouldn't be conserved.

p: Momentum (mass × velocity) is conserved in every collision with no outside forces. In an elastic collision, kinetic energy (KE = ½mv²) is also conserved, so nothing is lost to heat, sound or bending.

When two objects of equal mass collide head-on elastically and one starts at rest, they simply exchange velocities. The moving one stops and the resting one takes off at the same speed. Billiard balls come close to this.
If the collision is inelastic, some kinetic energy is lost, and the balls won't fully swap.

mem: Elastic: momentum and KE both conserved
Inelastic: only momentum conserved
Equal masses, head-on, elastic: velocities swap
d_4A_18.trap: Using the inelastic, 'split the speed' result for a collision that's labeled elastic.
d_4A_18.plain: Think of Newton's cradle, the desk toy with hanging steel balls: swing one ball in, and exactly one ball swings out on the other side.

fig.cap: An ideal machine lowers the force by raising the distance; the work stays the same.
fig.alt: Movable pulley halving the effort while doubling the rope pulled.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. 80 N over 2 m is what lifting the load with no machine at all would take. A movable pulley shares the load between two rope segments, so you need less force.
Not quite. 40 N over 2 m is 40 × 2 = 80 J of work, but lifting 80 N by 2 m takes 80 × 2 = 160 J. Getting 160 J out for 80 J in would create energy from nothing. The rope has to go twice as far.

Correct. Two rope segments hold the load, so each carries half: 80 ÷ 2 = 40 N. To raise the load 2 m, both segments must shorten 2 m, so you pull 4 m of rope. Work in: 40 × 4 = 160 J. Work out: 80 × 2 = 160 J. They match.
Not quite. 160 N over 1 m reverses the trade: it doubles the force and halves the distance. The work is still 160 × 1 = 160 J, but that's not how a movable pulley works. It lowers the force you need.

p: Work is force times the distance moved along the force: W = F × d. A simple machine like a pulley changes how much force you need, but in the ideal (frictionless) case it can't change the work. Work in equals work out.

A movable pulley hangs on a loop of rope, so the load is held up by two rope segments. Each segment carries half the weight, so you only need to pull with half the force. In exchange, you pull twice as much rope.
That's the general rule: if a machine cuts the force by some factor, you have to move that many times farther.

mem: Ideal machine: work in = work out
Movable pulley: half the force, twice the rope
Machines trade force for distance

fm.f: W = F × d, where W = work, F = force, d = distance moved along the force
fm.v: Lifting the load: F = 80 N, d = 2 m. Pulling the rope: F = 80 ÷ 2 = 40 N, d = 2 × 2 = 4 m. W = ?
fm.s: Load: W = 80 × 2 = 160 J. Rope: W = 40 × 4 = 160 J. They match.
fm.why: In an ideal machine the work you put in equals the work done on the load.
fm.nc: 8 × 2 = 16, then add the zero: 160. And 4 × 4 = 16, add the zero: 160.

steps: Write the formula: W = F × d.
Find the force with a movable pulley: two segments share the load, so F = 80 N ÷ 2 = 40 N.
Find the rope pulled: both segments shorten by 2 m, so d = 2 × 2 = 4 m.
Work on the load: 80 N × 2 m = 160 J.
Work you do: 40 N × 4 m = 160 J. Equal, so the answer is 40 N and 4 m.
d_4A_23.trap: Thinking a machine reduces the work. It only trades force for distance.
d_4A_23.plain: Climbing a long, gentle ramp is easier than climbing a steep one, but you walk farther to get to the same height.

fig.cap: Complementary angles (30° and 60°) give the same range; 45° gives the most with no drag. Air drag shortens the range and lowers the best angle.

ox: Not quite. The 30° ball doesn't go farther. Range depends on sin(2θ): sin 60° for the 30° launch and sin 120° for the 60° launch, and those are equal. A flatter throw moves faster sideways but lands sooner, and it evens out.

Correct. Range depends on sin(2θ). For 30°, that's sin 60°; for 60°, it's sin 120°, which is the same number. So the ranges are equal. Height depends on sin²θ, and sin 60° is bigger than sin 30°, so the 60° ball climbs higher.
Not quite. Both parts are off. The ranges are equal, not bigger for 60°, and the heights aren't equal: the steeper launch puts more speed into going up, so it rises higher.

Not quite. The ranges are equal, but the paths aren't the same. The 60° ball sends more of its speed upward, so it rises higher and stays in the air longer, while the 30° ball stays low and moves faster sideways.

concept.t: Range and height for different launch angles
p: The launch angle θ is measured up from the ground. On level ground with no air resistance, the range (how far away it lands) depends on sin(2θ). That's biggest at θ = 45°, because sin 90° = 1.
Two angles that add up to 90°, like 30° and 60° or 20° and 70°, give the same range. One is a low, fast, short flight; the other is a high, slow, long flight.
Maximum height depends on sin²θ, which is the upward part of the launch speed, squared. The steeper launch always goes higher, even when the ranges are the same.

mem: Range depends on sin(2θ); biggest at 45°
Angles adding to 90° give equal range
Height depends on sin²θ: steeper goes higher
d_4A_30.trap: Thinking a bigger angle always means a longer range. Range peaks at 45° and is the same for angles adding up to 90°.
d_4A_30.plain: A basketball lobbed high and one shot on a flatter arc can land in the same spot. The lob just gets higher on the way.

fig.cap: Flow rate Q = A·v is the same at every level of the circulation, so blood is slowest where the total area is largest: the capillaries.
fig.alt: Total cross-sectional area and average blood speed from aorta to venae cavae.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Illustrative areas.

ox: Not quite. One capillary is very narrow, which makes this tempting. But there are billions of them side by side, and speed depends on their combined area, which is huge. So the blood slows down.

Not quite. Blood pressure isn't constant around the circuit; it falls steadily from the aorta to the veins. And blood speed isn't set by pressure being constant; it's set by continuity, flow = area × speed.
Not quite. Capillary resistance is high, and that causes a pressure drop. But how fast blood moves at each level depends on the total cross-sectional area, not on the resistance.

Correct. Continuity says A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. The total capillary area is about 1000 times the aorta's, so the speed is about 1000 times lower: v₂ = v₁ ÷ 1000. Slow flow gives O₂ and nutrients time to move into the tissues.

p: Flow rate is the volume of blood passing a point each second. Blood can't be squeezed, so in a closed loop the flow rate is the same at every level: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. A is the cross-sectional area (the size of the opening blood flows through) and v is the speed.

For vessels side by side, like capillaries, use the TOTAL area of all of them. A single capillary is far narrower than the aorta, but there are so many that their combined area is about 1000 times bigger.
So blood is fastest in the aorta and slowest in the capillaries. That slow pace is useful: it gives oxygen, nutrients and waste time to cross the thin capillary walls.

mem: A × v = constant (flow rate)
Capillaries: biggest total area, slowest blood
Aorta: fastest; capillaries: slowest

fm.f: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, where A = total cross-sectional area, v = average blood speed, 1 = aorta, 2 = capillaries
fm.v: A₂ = 1000 × A₁; v₁ = aortic speed; v₂ = ?
fm.s: A₁ × v₁ = 1000 × A₁ × v₂; cancel A₁: v₁ = 1000 × v₂, so v₂ = v₁ ÷ 1000
fm.why: Blood can't be squeezed, so the same volume per second passes every level.
fm.nc: A₁ is on both sides, so it cancels and you don't need its actual value.

steps: Write the formula: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
Write down the values: A₂ = 1000 × A₁; v₁ is the aortic speed; v₂ is what we want.
Plug in: A₁ × v₁ = 1000 × A₁ × v₂.
Cancel A₁ from both sides: v₁ = 1000 × v₂.
Divide both sides by 1000: v₂ = v₁ ÷ 1000. Capillary blood moves about 1000 times slower.
d_4B_1.trap: Looking at one capillary's tiny radius instead of the total area of all the capillaries together.
d_4B_1.plain: A river rushing through a narrow channel slows to a crawl when it spreads out into a wide marsh.

fig.cap: In a constriction, continuity raises the speed (¼ area → 4× speed) and Bernoulli lowers the static pressure.
fig.alt: Tube with a constriction, flow speeds and manometer heights.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. The same flow squeezes through a smaller area, so blood speeds up (continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂). Bernoulli's principle then says that in a level vessel, faster flow goes with LOWER pressure, because P + ½ρv² stays constant.
Not quite. Faster flow doesn't come with higher pressure in a level tube. Bernoulli's principle says the energy of motion (½ρv²) goes up at the expense of pressure, so the pressure drops.
Not quite. The narrowing makes blood go FASTER, not slower, because the same volume per second has to fit through a smaller opening. Blood slows down where a vessel widens.
Not quite. The pressure part is right, but the speed is wrong. A narrowing speeds blood up. Narrow means fast, and fast means low pressure.

concept.t: Continuity and Bernoulli in a narrowed vessel
p: The continuity equation says the volume of fluid passing each point per second stays the same: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Where the vessel narrows (smaller A), the fluid must speed up (bigger v).

Bernoulli's equation is energy conservation for a flowing fluid. For a level tube: P + ½ρv² = constant. P is the pressure on the walls and ½ρv² is the energy of motion packed into each bit of volume. When one goes up, the other goes down.
Put them together: narrow → fast → low pressure. That's why a narrowed artery can have lower pressure at the narrowing itself, even though it seems 'squeezed'.

mem: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (narrow → fast)
Bernoulli (level): P + ½ρv² = constant (fast → low pressure)
Narrow = fast = low pressure

fm.f: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, where A = cross-sectional area of the vessel, v = blood speed, 1 = normal segment, 2 = narrowed segment
fm.v: Example: the narrowing has half the area, A₂ = ½A₁; v₁ = 1 (any unit); v₂ = ?
fm.s: A₁ × 1 = ½A₁ × v₂; cancel A₁: 1 = ½ × v₂, so v₂ = 2. The speed doubles. Then P + ½ρv² is constant, so a bigger v means a smaller P.
fm.why: Continuity tells you how the speed changes; Bernoulli turns that speed change into a pressure change.
fm.nc: Half the area means double the speed.

steps: Write the continuity formula: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
Write down example values: A₂ = ½A₁ and v₁ = 1.
Plug in and cancel A₁: 1 = ½ × v₂, so v₂ = 2. The blood speeds up.
Write Bernoulli for a level vessel: P + ½ρv² = constant.
Speed went up, so ½ρv² went up, so P must go down.
d_4B_3.sc: Area down → speed up (continuity). Speed up → pressure down (Bernoulli). No numbers needed.
d_4B_3.trap: Thinking a narrowing raises pressure because it feels squeezed. The pressure in the fast, narrow part is actually lower.
d_4B_3.plain: Put your thumb over the end of a garden hose and the water shoots out faster. That fast-moving water presses less on the sides, so its pressure is lower.

fig.cap: Myoglobin's hyperbolic curve has a low P50 (high affinity); hemoglobin's cooperativity gives an S-shaped curve that unloads O₂ in tissues.
fig.alt: Myoglobin and hemoglobin O₂ saturation curves.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Hill equation.

ox: Correct. Myoglobin has ONE heme and no cooperativity, so its binding curve is a hyperbola. Its P50 is about 2 mmHg, so it holds O₂ tightly even at very low PO₂. That higher affinity lets it take O₂ from hemoglobin and store it in muscle.
Not quite. An S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve with lower affinity describes hemoglobin: four subunits working together, with a P50 of about 26 mmHg. Myoglobin is the opposite on both counts.

Not quite. Myoglobin does have higher affinity, but its curve can't be S-shaped. The S shape comes from cooperativity, where binding at one subunit makes the others bind more easily. Myoglobin has only one subunit.

Not quite. The hyperbolic shape is right, but the affinity is backward. Myoglobin's P50 (about 2 mmHg) is far below hemoglobin's (about 26 mmHg), which means HIGHER affinity. If it were lower, it couldn't pull O₂ away from hemoglobin.

p: Hemoglobin, in red blood cells, has four subunits, each with a heme that binds one O₂. Binding one O₂ makes the others bind more easily. This teamwork is called cooperativity, and it gives an S-shaped (sigmoidal) binding curve. Hemoglobin's P50 is about 26 mmHg.
Myoglobin, in muscle, has just one subunit and one heme, so there's no teamwork. Its curve is a simple hyperbola. Its P50 is about 2 mmHg.

P50 is the PO₂ at which the protein is half full of O₂. Lower P50 means higher affinity, and the curve sits further left. Myoglobin's high affinity lets it take O₂ from hemoglobin and hold it as a backup supply, releasing it only when muscle PO₂ drops very low.

mem: Myoglobin: 1 heme, hyperbolic, P50 ≈ 2 mmHg, stores O₂ in muscle
Hemoglobin: 4 hemes, sigmoidal, P50 ≈ 26 mmHg, delivers O₂
Lower P50 = higher affinity = curve further left
d_4B_10.sc: A smaller P50 means it grabs O₂ harder, so its curve sits further to the left.
d_4B_10.mn: Myoglobin = Muscle's bank (stores O₂). Hemoglobin = hauls O₂ and hands it off.
d_4B_10.trap: Giving the S-shaped curve to a protein with only one subunit.
d_4B_10.plain: Myoglobin is a warehouse that hangs on tight to its oxygen. Hemoglobin is a delivery truck that drops oxygen off wherever it's needed.

fig.cap: Flow scales with r⁴, so a 16% narrower vessel carries half the flow. A narrow segment in series takes most of the pressure drop.
fig.alt: Flow against vessel radius with the baseline, norepinephrine and acetylcholine points.
