ox: Not quite. How much oxygen blood carries has nothing to do with how easily it flows through a tube. Flow depends on the pressure difference, radius, length and viscosity, and the viscosity went up.
Not quite. The radius is unchanged, but the viscosity isn't. More red cells make the blood thicker, so the flow changes even with the same radius.
Correct. Poiseuille: Q = ΔPπr⁴ ÷ (8ηL). ΔP, r and L stay the same, but η (viscosity) rises with hematocrit. η is on the bottom, so Q falls. Thicker blood is harder to push.
Not quite. Density (mass per volume) isn't part of Poiseuille's law. Viscosity (how thick and sticky a fluid is) is what rises with more red cells, and it lowers flow.

p: Poiseuille's law gives the flow rate of a thick fluid through a tube: Q = ΔPπr⁴ ÷ (8ηL). Flow goes up with the pressure difference ΔP and, very strongly, with the radius r (to the fourth power). Flow goes down with the viscosity η and the length L.
Resistance is how hard it is to push fluid through: R = 8ηL ÷ (πr⁴), and Q = ΔP ÷ R. So higher viscosity means higher resistance and less flow for the same push.
Blood's viscosity depends heavily on hematocrit, the share of blood made up of red cells. In polycythemia, there are too many red cells, the blood gets thicker, and it flows less easily.

mem: Poiseuille: Q = ΔPπr⁴ ÷ (8ηL)
Flow ∝ r⁴ and ∝ 1/η
Higher hematocrit → higher viscosity → lower flow

fm.f: Q = ΔPπr⁴ / (8ηL), where Q = flow rate, ΔP = pressure difference, r = vessel radius, η = viscosity, L = vessel length
fm.v: ΔP, r and L: unchanged; η: goes up; Q = ?
fm.s: Everything else is fixed, so Q ∝ 1/η. Example: if η doubles, Q becomes 1/2 of what it was.
fm.why: Poiseuille's law shows how each property of the vessel and the fluid changes flow.
fm.nc: η is on the bottom of the fraction, so a bigger η makes a smaller Q.

steps: Write the formula: Q = ΔPπr⁴ ÷ (8ηL).
Note the values: ΔP, r and L are unchanged; η is higher because there are more red cells.
η sits on the bottom of the fraction, so Q ∝ 1/η.
A bigger η means a smaller Q: flow decreases. (If η doubled, Q would halve.)
d_4B_12.sc: Change one thing at a time. With the pressure and tube fixed, flow moves opposite to viscosity.
d_4B_12.mn: Radius to the fourth rules the tube; thicker fluid flows slower.
d_4B_12.trap: Thinking more red cells means more flow because more oxygen is carried. Flow here is about fluid mechanics, not oxygen delivery.
d_4B_12.plain: Blood with too many red cells is like switching from water to syrup. It moves more slowly through the same straw with the same push.

fig.cap: Filtration at the arteriole end slightly exceeds reabsorption at the venule end; lymphatics return the excess fluid.
fig.alt: Capillary with filtration, reabsorption and lymphatic drainage.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. Oxygen is carried by the blood, mostly bound to hemoglobin in red cells. Lymph vessels don't deliver oxygen to tissues.

Not quite. Oncotic pressure is the inward pull on water from proteins in the plasma. Lymph doesn't raise it directly. By returning leaked protein to the blood, lymph only helps keep the balance indirectly.

Correct. Capillaries filter out more fluid than they reabsorb. Lymph vessels collect the leftover fluid and leaked protein from the tissue spaces and return them to the veins, keeping the tissues from swelling.
Not quite. Lymph vessels begin as tiny dead-end tubes in the tissue spaces between cells (the interstitium). They don't take water out of arterioles.

concept.t: How the lymphatic system keeps fluid in balance
p: Capillaries are leaky. At the start of a capillary, blood pressure pushes fluid out into the interstitium (the space between cells). Along the way, the pull of plasma proteins draws most of it back in. But filtration is a little bigger than reabsorption, so some fluid is always left behind, along with a small amount of leaked protein.

The lymphatic system handles that leftover. It's a one-way network of vessels that starts as tiny tubes in the tissues. It soaks up the extra fluid and protein (now called lymph), carries it through lymph nodes, and empties it into large veins near the heart.
If lymph drainage is blocked, the extra fluid piles up in the tissues and they swell. That swelling is called edema.

mem: Filtration is bigger than reabsorption; lymph returns the leftover
Lymph also returns leaked protein
Blocked lymph → edema
d_4B_17.trap: Forgetting that capillaries filter out more than they take back, which is why a drain is needed at all.
d_4B_17.plain: Picture a sink where the faucet runs a little faster than the drain. Without a second drain it would overflow. Lymph vessels are that second drain, keeping the floor dry.

p: A galvanic cell (a battery) uses a reaction that happens on its own to make electricity. The reaction is split in two: one electrode gives up electrons and the other takes them, and the electrons travel through a wire in between. That moving stream of electrons is the electric current that powers things.

Oxidation means losing electrons, and it happens at the anode. Reduction means gaining electrons, and it happens at the cathode. So electrons always go out of the anode, through the wire, and into the cathode. In a galvanic cell the anode is the negative end and the cathode is the positive end.

Watch out for 'conventional current'. Old diagrams draw current as moving from + to −, which is the opposite of how electrons actually move. If a question asks about electrons, they always go anode to cathode.

p: An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy from outside to force a reaction that wouldn't happen on its own. Chemists call that kind of reaction nonspontaneous. For it, ΔG (the free energy change) is positive and E°cell is negative. Charging a phone and plating silver onto a spoon are both examples.

The electrode jobs never change: reduction (gaining electrons) at the cathode, oxidation (losing electrons) at the anode. In both kinds of cell, electrons travel through the wire from the anode to the cathode.

What does flip is the sign. In a galvanic cell the cathode is positive. In an electrolytic cell the power source pushes electrons onto the cathode, so it's negative, and pulls them off the anode, so it's positive.

concept.t: Linking cell voltage, free energy and K
p: E° is the standard cell potential, the voltage a cell makes under standard conditions. ΔG° is the standard free energy change: if it's negative, the reaction is spontaneous, meaning it runs on its own. K is the equilibrium constant: if it's bigger than 1, there are more products than reactants once the reaction settles.

Two equations tie them together: ΔG° = −nFE° and ΔG° = −RT ln K. Here n is the number of moles of electrons moved, F is the Faraday constant, R is the gas constant and T is the temperature. All four are always positive, so only the signs of E°, ΔG° and ln K matter.
Put together: positive E° goes with negative ΔG° and K greater than 1. Negative E° goes with positive ΔG° and K less than 1. And E° = 0 goes with ΔG° = 0 and K = 1.

mem: E° > 0 ⇔ ΔG° < 0 ⇔ K > 1: spontaneous
E° < 0 ⇔ ΔG° > 0 ⇔ K < 1: nonspontaneous
ΔG° = −nFE° = −RT ln K

fm.f: ΔG° = −nFE°, where ΔG° = standard free energy change, n = moles of electrons moved, F = Faraday constant, E° = standard cell potential
fm.v: E° is positive; n and F are always positive; sign of ΔG° = ?
fm.s: ΔG° = −(positive)(positive)(positive) = negative; then −RT ln K = negative, so ln K is positive and K > 1
fm.why: This equation turns a voltage into a free energy, so the sign of E° sets the sign of ΔG°.
fm.nc: Only the signs matter here, so there's no arithmetic.

steps: Write the formula: ΔG° = −nFE°.
Write down the values: E° is positive, and n and F are always positive.
Plug in the signs: ΔG° = −(positive)(positive)(positive), which is negative.
Write the second formula: ΔG° = −RT ln K, with R and T always positive.
ΔG° is negative, so −RT ln K is negative, which means ln K is positive.
ln K is positive only when K is greater than 1. So ΔG° is negative and K > 1.

p: A galvanic cell lets a spontaneous reaction, one that runs on its own, release energy as electricity. A battery powering a flashlight is galvanic. Its ΔG (free energy change) is negative.
An electrolytic cell does the opposite. It uses energy from an outside source to force a reaction that wouldn't happen on its own, with ΔG positive.

A rechargeable battery is both, at different times. Discharging, it's galvanic. Charging, the charger pushes the reaction backward, so it's electrolytic. In both modes, reduction is at the cathode and oxidation at the anode.

Not quite. Electrons always travel from the anode, where they're released, to the cathode, where they're used. Cathode to anode is backward.

p: A concentration cell uses the same metal and the same ion on both sides, only at different concentrations. Because the two half-reactions are identical, the standard voltage E° is 0. But the cell still runs, because nature pushes the two concentrations to even out.

The dilute side needs more ions, so metal there is oxidized into ions. Oxidation means it's the anode. The concentrated side has too many ions, so ions there are reduced into metal. Reduction means it's the cathode.

Electrons go from anode to cathode, so they flow from the dilute side to the concentrated side. The cell keeps running until both sides have the same concentration, and then the voltage drops to zero.

ox: Correct. Hydrogen's levels crowd closer together as n goes up, so the gap from 2 to 1 is bigger than the gap from 3 to 2. A bigger gap gives a photon with more energy, and since E = hc/λ, more energy means a shorter wavelength.
Not quite. The pairing is right (less energy goes with a longer wavelength), but it's the wrong photon. The 2 → 1 drop is the big one, so it gives more energy, not less.
Not quite. Energy and wavelength always move in opposite directions, because E = hc/λ puts λ on the bottom. A more energetic photon has to have a shorter wavelength.
Not quite. Each drop gives a photon with energy equal to its own gap, and the gaps are different sizes. The 2 → 1 gap is about five times bigger than the 3 → 2 gap, so the photons are very different.

p: An electron in a hydrogen atom can only sit in certain energy levels, numbered n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. n = 1 is the lowest, closest to the nucleus.
The levels aren't evenly spaced. They're far apart near n = 1 and crowd closer together as n goes up. So drops that end at n = 1 are the biggest, and drops between high levels are small.

When an electron drops, it gives off a photon whose energy equals the gap. Photon energy is E = hc/λ, where h and c are constants and λ is the wavelength. So big drops give high-energy, short-wavelength light (ultraviolet for drops to n = 1), and smaller drops give lower-energy, longer-wavelength light (visible for drops to n = 2).

mem: Photon energy = the gap between the two levels
Gaps shrink as n goes up
More energy means shorter wavelength

ox: Correct. Ionization energy rises from left to right across a row as protons are added. Neon is the noble gas at the end of row 2, with a full shell held tightly, so it has the highest ionization energy here.
Not quite. Sodium has a single outer electron sitting outside a full shell, far from the nucleus. It comes off easily, so sodium has one of the lowest ionization energies of all.
Not quite. Magnesium is a metal, and metals give up their outer electrons fairly easily. Its ionization energy is much lower than the nonmetals' at the right of the table.

Not quite. Fluorine's ionization energy is high, but neon sits one step to the right in the same row, with one more proton pulling on a full shell. So neon is higher. The trap is mixing this up with electronegativity, where fluorine is the top.

p: First ionization energy is the energy needed to pull the outermost electron off a gas atom. The tighter an atom holds that electron, the higher its ionization energy.

Across a row, left to right, each element adds a proton while its outer electrons stay in the same shell. The pull gets stronger, so ionization energy rises. Going up a column, atoms get smaller and their outer electrons sit closer to the nucleus, so ionization energy rises too.
That puts the highest values at the top right of the table. Helium is the highest of all, followed by neon. Noble gases, with full shells, are the hardest to ionize in their row.

mem: Ionization energy rises left to right and bottom to top
Noble gases are highest in their row
Metals lose electrons easily

d_4E_14.plain: Think of pulling a toy out of a child's hand. The one with the tightest, two-handed grip (neon) is the hardest to win against.

ox: Not quite. Neon already has a full outer shell. An extra electron would have to start a whole new shell, far from the nucleus, so neon releases little or no energy. Its electron affinity is about zero or even unfavorable.
Not quite. Sodium does release a small amount of energy gaining an electron, but very little. It has one lonely outer electron and much prefers to give it away.
Not quite. Magnesium's 3s subshell is full, so a new electron would have to go into the higher-energy 3p. That isn't favorable, and its electron affinity is about zero or slightly unfavorable.

Correct. Chlorine is one electron short of a full outer shell, so gaining one releases a lot of energy. Its electron affinity is the most exothermic of any element, slightly more than fluorine's, whose small size crowds the new electron.

p: Electron affinity is the energy change when a gas atom gains one electron. If energy is released (exothermic, a negative number), the atom is happy to take it. If energy has to be put in, it isn't.

Halogens, like F and Cl, are one electron short of a full outer shell, so they have the most exothermic electron affinities. Atoms with full shells or full subshells, like the noble gases and group 2 metals, don't want an extra electron, so theirs are near zero or unfavorable.
The one surprise: chlorine beats fluorine. Fluorine is so small that a new electron is crowded by the ones already there, so it releases slightly less energy.

mem: Halogens have the most exothermic electron affinities
Chlorine edges out fluorine
Noble gases and group 2 are near zero

ox: Correct. The three 2p orbitals have equal energy, so Hund's rule applies: one electron goes into each before any pair up, and all three spin the same way. Nitrogen ends up with three unpaired electrons.
Not quite. Putting two electrons in one orbital while another sits empty forces them close together, so they repel more. Hund's rule says they spread out first. Pairing too early is the trap.
Not quite. Separate orbitals is right, but in the lowest-energy arrangement, all the single electrons spin the same way. Mixing spins up loses the small extra stability that same-spin electrons get.
Not quite. A pair is two electrons, so three electrons can make at most one pair plus one single. And Hund's rule says they shouldn't pair at all while an empty orbital is available.

p: Within a subshell, all the orbitals have the same energy. The 2p subshell has three such orbitals, and each can hold up to two electrons, which must spin in opposite directions if they share.

Hund's rule says electrons fill these equal-energy orbitals one at a time, all spinning the same way, before any orbital gets a second electron. Electrons repel each other, so spreading out keeps them farther apart, and same-spin electrons get a little extra stability on top of that.
So nitrogen, 1s² 2s² 2p³, has one electron in each 2p orbital and three unpaired electrons. Atoms with unpaired electrons are pulled toward a magnet, which is called being paramagnetic.

Pair up only once every orbital has one electron

ox: Not quite. This has two mistakes. London dispersion is placed first, but for small molecules it's the weakest force. And hydrogen bonds are placed above ion–dipole, but a full charge pulling on a polar molecule beats a hydrogen bond. Ion–dipole above dipole–dipole is the one part it gets right.
Not quite. Ordinary dipole–dipole forces are weaker than both ion–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds, so they can't be first. And hydrogen bonds are strong, so they can't be last.

Correct. Ion–dipole is strongest because a full charge is involved. Hydrogen bonds come next, then ordinary dipole–dipole forces between permanent partial charges, then London dispersion, which comes from short-lived dipoles.
Not quite. This flips two pairs. Ion–dipole beats hydrogen bonds, because a full charge pulls harder than a partial one. And for small molecules, dipole–dipole beats dispersion.

p: Intermolecular forces are attractions between separate particles. The more charge involved, the stronger the pull. An ion carries a full charge, so ion–dipole forces (an ion attracting one end of a polar molecule) are the strongest of these.

A hydrogen bond is a strong kind of dipole–dipole force between an H on N, O or F and a lone pair on another N, O or F. Ordinary dipole–dipole forces between other polar molecules are weaker. London dispersion forces come from electrons briefly bunching up on one side; every molecule has them, and they're weakest for small molecules but grow with size.

mem: Ion–dipole > hydrogen bond > dipole–dipole > London dispersion
Hydrogen bonds need H on N, O or F
Dispersion grows with molecule size and electron count

Not quite. Phosphates are part of the sugar–phosphate backbone, not the base pairs. Every nucleotide has one, whatever its base, so A–T-rich DNA doesn't have more of them.
Not quite. G and A are both purines, the bases with two rings. The pyrimidines, with one ring, are C, T and U. And even if it were true, it wouldn't explain the difference in melting temperature.

Guanine pairs with cytosine using three hydrogen bonds. Adenine pairs with thymine using two. G–C pairs also stack more tightly on their neighbors. So the more G–C pairs a DNA has, the more heat it takes to separate the strands, and the higher its Tm.

More G–C = higher melting temperature
Purines: A, G. Pyrimidines: C, T, U

ox: Correct. For water, the solid–liquid line slopes backward (a negative slope), because ice is less dense than liquid water. Raising the pressure at a temperature just below 0 °C carries you across that line into the liquid region, so the ice melts.

Not quite. The triple point is where solid, liquid and gas all coexist, and for water it's actually at a very low pressure. Its location doesn't explain why squeezing ice melts it; the slope of the solid–liquid line does.
Not quite. The critical point is where liquid and gas stop being different and become one fluid. It has nothing to do with ice turning into liquid.
Not quite. The sublimation curve, between solid and gas, slopes upward, not flat. And this question is about solid turning to liquid, not solid turning to gas.

p: A phase diagram plots pressure (going up) against temperature (going across). Each region shows which phase is stable, and each line shows where two phases can exist together.

For most substances, like CO₂, the solid–liquid line leans to the right, because the solid is denser and pressure favors the denser phase. Water is unusual: ice is less dense than liquid water (that's why ice floats). So pressure favors the liquid, the line leans left, and squeezing ice can melt it.

mem: Water's solid–liquid line has a negative slope
Ice is less dense than liquid water
Pressure favors the denser phase
d_5B_20.trap: Assuming the solid–liquid line always slopes forward, as it does for most substances like CO₂.
d_5B_20.plain: Ice takes up more room than the same water as a liquid. Squeeze it, and it would rather become the more compact liquid.

ox: Not quite. When one atom takes the electrons completely, that's an ionic bond, like Na⁺ and Cl⁻. In H₃N–BF₃ the pair is still shared between nitrogen and boron, so it's covalent.

Correct. Nitrogen in NH₃ has a lone pair it isn't using. Boron in BF₃ has only six electrons and an empty p orbital. Nitrogen gives both electrons of its lone pair to boron, so N is the Lewis base (it donates the pair) and B is the Lewis acid (it accepts it).
Not quite. One electron from each atom is how an ordinary covalent bond forms, like the H–H bond in H₂. What makes a coordinate bond special is that one atom supplies both electrons.
Not quite. The shared pair sits between nitrogen and boron. The fluorines are attached to boron, but they didn't donate this pair and it isn't spread over them.

p: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. Most of the time each atom puts in one electron. In a coordinate (also called dative) bond, one atom puts in both.

That usually happens between a Lewis base, an atom with a lone pair to give, and a Lewis acid, an atom with an empty orbital that wants one. Boron in BF₃ has only six electrons around it, so it happily takes the lone pair from the nitrogen in NH₃.
After the bond forms, you can't tell it apart from a regular covalent bond. You'll see the same idea when metal ions bind water or ammonia, and when hemoglobin's iron binds O₂.

mem: Coordinate bond: both electrons come from one atom
Lewis base gives the pair; Lewis acid takes it
Once formed, it acts like any covalent bond
x5B_004.trap: Thinking a coordinate bond is a different kind of bond once it's formed. It only differs in where the electrons came from.
x5B_004.plain: Two friends share a sandwich. Usually each brings half. In a coordinate bond, one friend brought the whole sandwich and the other just brought an empty plate.

fig.cap: Bond formation releases energy: potential energy falls to a minimum at the bond length, then rises steeply as nuclei repel.
fig.alt: Potential energy of two H atoms against distance, minimum at 74 pm and −436 kJ/mol.

ox: Not quite. Making a bond releases energy, so the energy of the system goes down as the atoms come together, not up. A curve that rises and then stays flat would mean bonding costs energy, which is backward.

Not quite. It's true that no electrons are gained or lost, but that doesn't keep the energy constant. Each electron feels the pull of both nuclei once the atoms are close, and that extra attraction lowers the energy.
Not quite. The energy does fall at first, but it can't keep falling. When the nuclei get closer than the bond length, the two positive charges push each other away strongly and the energy shoots up.

Correct. The energy drops as the atoms approach and reaches its minimum at the bond length, where attraction and repulsion balance. Closer than that, the nuclei repel and the energy climbs steeply. The depth of that dip is the bond energy, the energy you'd need to pull the atoms apart again.

concept.t: The energy curve of a bond
p: Potential energy is stored energy that depends on where things are. Two H atoms far apart don't interact, so their energy is set at zero. As they move closer, each electron starts feeling the pull of both nuclei, and the energy goes down.

At one distance, the bond length, the pulls and pushes balance and the energy is as low as it gets. For H₂ that's about 74 pm. If the atoms get closer still, the two positive nuclei repel and the energy rises fast.
Plot energy against distance and you get a well shape. The bottom of the well tells you the bond length. The depth of the well is the bond energy: how much energy it takes to break the bond.

mem: Bottom of the energy well = bond length
Depth of the well = bond energy
Too close: the nuclei repel and energy shoots up
x5B_005.trap: Picking 'decreases continuously'. Repulsion between the nuclei at short range makes the curve turn back up.
x5B_005.plain: Two magnets pulled together settle into a sweet spot. Try to push them any closer and something shoves back.

fig.cap: DNA moves toward the anode; distance falls linearly with log(size). Supercoiled plasmid usually runs fastest.
fig.alt: Agarose gel with a size ladder and the three forms of a plasmid.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. Both parts are backward. DNA is negative, so it moves toward the positive anode, not the cathode. And larger fragments get caught in the gel more, so they move slower.
Not quite. The direction is right: DNA does move toward the anode. But big fragments keep getting tangled in the gel's pores, so they move slower than small ones, not faster.
Correct. DNA's phosphate backbone is negative, so it's pulled toward the positive anode. Smaller fragments wiggle through the gel's pores more easily, so they move faster and travel farther.
Not quite. The size part is right: smaller fragments do move faster. But DNA is negative, so it's pushed away from the negative cathode and pulled toward the positive anode.

p: Electrophoresis uses an electric field to move charged molecules through a gel. DNA has a negative charge from the phosphate groups in its backbone, so it moves toward the positive electrode, the anode.

The gel is a mesh of tiny pores. Small fragments slip through quickly, while large ones get slowed down. Since every DNA piece has about the same charge for its size, size is what sorts them. After the run, the smallest pieces are farthest from the starting wells.

mem: DNA is negative, so it moves to the anode (+)
Smaller fragments travel farther
All DNA has about the same charge for its size, so size decides speed
d_5C_21.mn: Opposites attract: negative DNA runs to the positive pole. Some people say 'run to red', since the positive lead is usually red.
d_5C_21.trap: Forgetting that DNA is negative, or flipping which size moves faster.
d_5C_21.plain: It's like running through a thick forest. A small kid darts between the trees fast, but a kid dragging a big sheet keeps getting snagged.

fig.cap: Below the triple-point temperature there is no liquid, so raising pressure turns gas directly to solid; a positive solid–liquid slope means the solid is denser.
fig.alt: Schematic phase diagram with triple point, critical point and a pressure arrow below the triple point.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph. Schematic.

ox: Not quite. Sublimation is for solids. Two liquids with close boiling points are separated by fractional distillation, which repeats the boiling and condensing many times.

Correct. A solid with a real vapor pressure below its melting point can turn straight into gas when warmed. On a cold surface it turns straight back into solid, as pure crystals. Impurities that can't vaporize stay behind in the bottom.
Not quite. To get a dissolved salt back, you evaporate the water or let the salt crystallize. Salts like NaCl hold together far too tightly to turn into a gas this way.
Not quite. Proteins are huge molecules that fall apart before they'd ever turn to gas. They're separated by methods like chromatography or electrophoresis.

p: Sublimation is a solid turning directly into a gas, skipping the liquid. Deposition is the reverse: a gas turning directly into a solid. Some solids, like iodine, caffeine and naphthalene, have enough vapor pressure to sublime when warmed gently, often under vacuum.

To purify one, you warm the impure solid under a cold surface called a cold finger. The compound turns to gas, then deposits as pure crystals on the cold surface. Anything that can't turn into a gas stays behind.

mem: Sublimation: solid straight to gas
Deposition: gas straight to solid
It works when the compound vaporizes easily and the impurities don't
d_5C_28.trap: Thinking sublimation only happens with dry ice. Many solids, like caffeine and iodine, can be purified this way.
d_5C_28.plain: It's like frost forming on a cold window: water vapor in the air skips being liquid and sticks to the glass as ice, while the dust stays behind.

fig.cap: The less dense solvent forms the top layer. Ionized forms move into water: NaHCO₃ takes carboxylic acids, NaOH also takes phenols, HCl takes amines.
fig.alt: Separatory funnels for ether and dichloromethane, and an acid–base extraction sequence.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. Two liquids that don't mix stack by density. Ether is 0.71 g/mL and water is 1.00 g/mL. 0.71 is less than 1.00, so the ether floats on top.
Not quite. Organic layers don't always sink. They sink only when they're denser than water, like dichloromethane (1.33 g/mL). Ether, at 0.71 g/mL, is lighter than water, so it floats.
Not quite. Polarity decides whether two liquids mix, not which one is on top. And the reasoning is backward anyway: ether is much less polar than water. The ether is on top because it's less dense.
Not quite. Ether and water mostly don't mix, so they separate into two layers. That's exactly why a separatory funnel works with them.

p: A separatory funnel is a glass funnel with a tap at the bottom, used to separate two liquids that don't mix. When you shake and then let them settle, they form two layers. The denser liquid, the one with more mass per mL, goes to the bottom.

Density is the only thing that decides which layer is on top. Water is 1.00 g/mL. Any liquid less dense than 1.00 floats on water, and any liquid denser than 1.00 sinks. So always compare the solvent's density with 1.00.

mem: Top layer = the less dense liquid
Water is 1.00 g/mL
Ether, hexane and ethyl acetate float on water
Dichloromethane and chloroform sink below water
x5C_002.trap: Assuming organic always means top. Compare the solvent's density with 1.00 g/mL.
x5C_002.plain: Oil floats on vinegar in a bottle of salad dressing. The lighter liquid always rides on top.

fig.alt: Separatory funnels for ether and dichloromethane, and an acid–base extraction sequence.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. This assumes organic solvents always float. Dichloromethane is 1.33 g/mL, which is more than water's 1.00 g/mL, so the organic layer is on the bottom. The top layer is the water.

Not quite. The bottom layer here is the dichloromethane, not the water. Water (1.00 g/mL) is lighter, so it's on top. And keeping the water layer would throw away the product, which moved into the organic layer.
Not quite. The product doesn't split evenly. A neutral organic compound strongly prefers the organic solvent, so almost all of it ends up in one layer.

Correct. Dichloromethane (1.33 g/mL) is denser than water (1.00 g/mL), so the organic layer sits at the bottom. The neutral product moved into it, so drain the bottom layer through the tap and keep it.

p: In an extraction, the product moves into the liquid it dissolves in best. A neutral organic product moves into the organic solvent. So you keep the organic layer.

Next, figure out which layer that is by comparing densities with water (1.00 g/mL). Solvents denser than water, like dichloromethane, form the bottom layer and drain out first. Solvents lighter than water, like ether, form the top layer.

mem: Bottom layer = the denser liquid
Dichloromethane is denser than water, so it's the bottom layer
Neutral organic products go into the organic layer
Never throw out a layer until you've found your product
x5C_003.trap: Assuming the organic layer is always on top. Check the density first.
x5C_003.plain: It's like knowing which shelf your toy is on. First figure out which liquid is heavier, and then you know which layer is at the bottom.

fig.cap: The less dense solvent forms the top layer. Ionized forms move into water: NaHCO₃ takes carboxylic acids, NaOH also takes phenols, HCl takes amines.
fig.alt: Separatory funnels for ether and dichloromethane, and an acid–base extraction sequence.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. Bicarbonate is a weak base. Its conjugate acid has a pKₐ of about 6.4, which is lower than the phenol's pKₐ of about 10, so it can't pull the phenol's H⁺ off. It's strong enough for carboxylic acids (pKₐ about 4 to 5) but not phenols.

Correct. Hydroxide is a strong base. Its conjugate acid, water, has a pKₐ of about 15.7, well above the phenol's 10. So OH⁻ pulls off the phenol's H⁺, making a charged phenoxide ion that dissolves in water. Naphthalene has no acidic H, so it stays in the ether.
Not quite. Adding acid keeps the phenol in its neutral, protonated form, so it stays in the ether. An HCl wash is used to pull bases, like amines, into water instead.
Not quite. Brine (saturated salt water) is used to pull dissolved water out of the organic layer. It isn't acidic or basic, so it doesn't change the phenol at all.

p: Neutral organic molecules dissolve in organic solvents like ether. Charged ions dissolve in water. To move an acid out of the ether and into water, you add a base that's strong enough to take its H⁺ and turn it into an ion.

How do you know if the base is strong enough? Compare pKₐ values. The base works when its conjugate acid has a higher pKₐ than the acid you're removing. A phenol has a pKₐ of about 10, so bicarbonate (about 6.4) fails and hydroxide (about 15.7) works.

mem: Carboxylic acid (pKₐ 4 to 5): NaHCO₃ is enough
Phenol (pKₐ about 10): needs NaOH
A base turns an acid into a water-soluble salt
HCl pulls amines into water
x5C_004.trap: Using bicarbonate for a phenol. It's too weak. Compare the pKₐ values.
x5C_004.plain: Think of putting a life vest on someone so they leave the oil pool and move to the water pool. Only a base strong enough to grab the H⁺ can put the vest on.

fig.cap: (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane has an internal mirror plane, so it is a meso compound identical to (2S,3R).
fig.alt: Meso 2,3-dibromobutane with stereocenters labeled.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. Each stereocenter holds H, Br, CH₃ and the other CHBr group, so the two halves of the molecule are built the same. In the R,S form a mirror plane cuts right through the middle, which makes it meso: it has stereocenters but isn't chiral. Number the chain from the other end and (2R,3S) reads as (2S,3R). Same molecule, two names.

Not quite. Enantiomers are mirror images that can't be stacked on top of each other, like your left and right hands. Flipping every center normally gives the enantiomer, which is why this is tempting. But a meso compound can be stacked on its own mirror image, so flipping both centers just hands you the same molecule back.
Not quite. A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of two chiral enantiomers. This molecule has an internal mirror plane, so it isn't chiral at all, and there's no mirror-image partner to pair it with.

Not quite. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that aren't mirror images, and they're truly different compounds with different properties. Here both centers flipped and the molecule is symmetric, so you end up with the identical compound, not a different one.

p: A stereocenter is a carbon holding four different groups. A molecule with stereocenters is usually chiral, meaning its mirror image is a different molecule. A meso compound is the exception: it has stereocenters but also a mirror plane through its middle, so its mirror image is itself.

Meso shows up when two stereocenters carry the same set of groups and have opposite labels (R,S). In 2,3-dibromobutane, (2R,3S) is meso. The R,R and S,S forms are the real enantiomer pair, so this compound has only 3 stereoisomers, not the 4 you'd expect from 2 centers.
A quick check: if you can draw a line through the molecule so one half reflects onto the other, it's meso.

mem: Meso: stereocenters plus an internal mirror plane, so not chiral
Two matching centers: meso has opposite labels (R,S)
2,3-dibromobutane: R,R and S,S enantiomers, plus one meso form
x5D_014.trap: Assuming opposite labels always mean enantiomers. If the two ends of the molecule match, R,S and S,R are the same molecule.
x5D_014.plain: Your hands are mirror images but not the same. A plain coffee mug is its own mirror image. A meso compound is the mug.

ox: Correct. In trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane one methyl points up and the other points down. On neighboring carbons of a chair, the two equatorial spots are also one up and one down, so both methyls can sit equatorial at the same time. Equatorial is the roomy position, so this chair is the comfortable one.

Not quite. In cis-1,2 both methyls point the same way, say both up. On neighboring carbons, the two 'up' spots are one axial and one equatorial. Flip the chair and they swap, but one is still axial. So cis-1,2 can never be both equatorial.

Not quite. Trans is the right answer for 1,2 and 1,4, but 1,3 is the odd one out. Carbons 1 and 3 are two steps apart, so the pattern flips: their two equatorial spots point the same way, which means cis-1,3 is the both-equatorial isomer. Trans-1,3 always has one axial methyl.

Not quite. For 1,4 the pattern is the same as for 1,2: the equatorial spots point one up, one down, so trans-1,4 is both equatorial. Cis-1,4 has both groups pointing the same way, which forces one of them axial in either chair.

concept.t: Chair shapes of rings with two groups
p: Cyclohexane, a ring of six carbons, folds into a 'chair' shape. Each carbon has one axial spot (straight up or down) and one equatorial spot (out to the side, around the ring's edge). Equatorial is roomier, so bigger groups prefer it. The chair can flip, which swaps every axial spot to equatorial and back.

Cis means two groups are on the same face of the ring; trans means opposite faces. Whether both groups can be equatorial depends on how far apart they are. For 1,2 and 1,4, trans works. For 1,3, cis works.
You don't need to draw the chair every time. Just remember that 1,3 is the reverse of the other two.

mem: 1,2: trans can be both equatorial
1,3: cis can be both equatorial
1,4: trans can be both equatorial
x5D_023.sc: Look at the second number. Even (2 or 4): trans can be both equatorial. Odd (3): cis can.
x5D_023.trap: Using one rule for every position. The 1,3 pattern is the reverse of 1,2 and 1,4.
x5D_023.plain: Think of a crowded dinner table. Everyone wants the seats with elbow room (equatorial), not the cramped ones squeezed up or down (axial).

fig.cap: The racemic acid reacts with one pure amine enantiomer to give two diastereomeric salts, (R)-acid·(R)-amine and (S)-acid·(R)-amine. Diastereomers have different solubilities, so one crystallizes out.
fig.alt: Resolution of a racemic carboxylic acid with an (R)-amine into two diastereomeric salts.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Not quite. The mirror image of an (R,R) salt would be (S,S), and that salt never forms here because the amine is only R. So (R,R) and (S,R) aren't enantiomers. And if they were, they'd have identical solubilities and couldn't be separated by crystallizing.

Not quite. Racemizing means scrambling a pure compound into a 50:50 mix of both mirror images. The amine just grabs a proton from the acid to make a salt; it doesn't touch the acid's stereocenter. And making the mix more scrambled would be the opposite of what you want.

Correct. The (R)-amine pairs with the R acid to give an (R,R) salt and with the S acid to give an (S,R) salt. These two are stereoisomers but not mirror images, so they're diastereomers. Diastereomers differ in solubility, so one crystallizes first and can be filtered off.

Not quite. An acid-base reaction like this isn't picky: both the R and S acids give up a proton to the amine and form salts. The separation works because the two salts that form have different solubilities.

p: Enantiomers are mirror-image molecules. They share every physical property in an ordinary setting: the same melting point, boiling point and solubility. That makes them very hard to separate directly.

Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, and they do have different physical properties. So the plan is to turn the pair of enantiomers into a pair of diastereomers by attaching a pure, one-handed partner.

Here a racemic acid (a 50:50 mix of R and S) reacts with a pure (R)-amine to make two salts. Crystallize out the less soluble salt, then add strong acid to break the salt and get back one pure enantiomer of the acid. This process is called resolution.

mem: Racemic acid + one-handed amine: two diastereomeric salts
Diastereomers have different solubilities, so crystallize
Add strong acid to get the pure acid back
x5D_025.trap: Calling the salts enantiomers. The amine's fixed handedness makes them diastereomers.
x5D_025.plain: A left glove and a right glove look like a matched pair. Put each one on the same right hand and suddenly one fits and one doesn't. Now you can tell them apart.

fig.cap: SN2 is one concerted backside attack (inversion, rate = k[RX][Nu]); SN1 goes through a planar carbocation (racemization, rate = k[RX], rearrangements).
fig.alt: SN2 inversion of (R)-2-bromobutane and the two-step SN1 pathway with conditions for each.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit.

ox: Not quite. A meso compound needs two or more stereocenters plus a mirror plane. The product, 3-methylhexan-3-ol, has just one stereocenter (C3 holds OH, methyl, ethyl and propyl), so it's chiral and can't be meso.

Correct. A tertiary bromide in water, a polar protic solvent, reacts by SN1. The bromide leaves first and makes a flat carbocation. Water can attack either face, so both R and S alcohols form. That gives a nearly racemic mix (often with a little extra inversion, because the leaving bromide briefly shields one face).

Not quite. Pure inversion, where the shape flips like an umbrella in the wind, is what SN2 gives. SN2 needs the nucleophile to hit the carbon from the back, and three carbon groups crowd that path on a tertiary carbon. So SN2 doesn't happen here.
Not quite. Pure retention would mean the product keeps the starting (S) shape. But the carbocation is flat and has no memory of which way the bromide pointed, so water comes in from both sides.

concept.t: What SN1 does to a stereocenter
p: In an SN1 reaction the leaving group leaves first, all on its own. What's left is a carbocation: a carbon with only three bonds and a positive charge. That carbon is flat (chemists call it sp²), like a triangle lying on a table.

A nucleophile, an electron-rich species looking for a positive center, then attacks. Since the carbocation is flat, it can come in from the top or the bottom. If you started with one pure enantiomer, you end up with both, a racemic or nearly racemic mix.

SN1 is favored by tertiary carbons (they make the most stable carbocations) and polar protic solvents like water. SN2 is the opposite: one smooth step with backside attack, giving inversion, and it works best on unhindered carbons.

mem: Tertiary carbon + water or alcohol solvent: SN1
Flat carbocation: attack from both faces, so racemization
SN2 gives inversion; SN1 gives racemization
x5D_027.trap: Picking inversion because it's the substitution result you know best. Inversion belongs to SN2.
x5D_027.plain: Picture a flat pancake on a plate. You can stab it with a fork from above or slide a spatula under it. Either side works, so you can't tell which side was 'up' to begin with.

fig.cap: SN2 is one concerted backside attack (inversion, rate = k[RX][Nu]); SN1 goes through a planar carbocation (racemization, rate = k[RX], rearrangements).
fig.alt: SN2 inversion of (R)-2-bromobutane and the two-step SN1 pathway with conditions for each.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit.

ox: Not quite. I⁻ is the best halide nucleophile in protic solvents like water or ethanol. There, small anions like F⁻ get wrapped in a shell of hydrogen bonds that slows them down, while big I⁻ is barely held. DMSO can't make those hydrogen bonds, so that advantage disappears and the order flips.

Correct. DMSO has no O–H or N–H, so it can't hydrogen bond to anions, and the anions are left bare. A bare anion's nucleophile strength follows its basicity. F⁻ is the strongest base of the four halides, so it's the strongest nucleophile in DMSO.
Not quite. Cl⁻ is in the middle. It's a weaker base than F⁻, so in a solvent with no hydrogen bonding it's a weaker nucleophile too.
Not quite. Br⁻ is a weaker base than both F⁻ and Cl⁻, so in DMSO it ranks below them. Only I⁻ is weaker.

concept.t: How the solvent changes nucleophile strength
p: A polar protic solvent has O–H or N–H bonds (water, alcohols). It surrounds anions with hydrogen bonds. Small anions like F⁻ hold their charge in a tiny space, so they get wrapped the tightest and are slowed the most. That's why I⁻ is the best halide nucleophile in water.

A polar aprotic solvent (DMSO, acetone, DMF) is polar but has no O–H or N–H. It surrounds the positive ions and leaves anions bare. Bare anions act according to basicity, so the order flips: F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻.
On the MCAT, always read the solvent before ranking nucleophiles.

mem: Protic solvent: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻
Aprotic solvent: F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻
Aprotic: nucleophile strength follows basicity
x5D_029.trap: Using the water order when the solvent is DMSO. Read the solvent first.
x5D_029.plain: In water, F⁻ is wrapped in a heavy blanket of water molecules and can barely move. In DMSO it has no blanket, so it runs around freely.

fig.cap: The absolute threshold is the intensity detected on 50% of trials. Weber's law: the just-noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the starting intensity.
fig.alt: Psychometric function and Weber's law lines for weight and brightness.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Illustrative values.

ox: Not quite. This describes the difference threshold, or just noticeable difference (JND). The JND compares two stimuli and asks how big a change has to be before you notice. The absolute threshold involves just one stimulus: can you detect it at all?

Not quite. Your nervous system always has some random background activity, called noise. Because of it, a faint stimulus is caught on some trials and missed on others. There's no faint intensity you'd detect 100% of the time, so 50% is used.
Correct. The absolute threshold is the lowest intensity of a stimulus that a person detects 50% of the time. Detection is probabilistic near that level, so the halfway point is used as the cutoff.
Not quite. The point where a stimulus starts to hurt is the pain threshold. The absolute threshold is about first being able to notice something, not about pain.

p: The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus a person can notice, like the softest sound or dimmest light. Near that level, the same stimulus is noticed on some tries and missed on others, because the nervous system is noisy.
So researchers define it as the intensity detected half the time (50%). Don't confuse it with the difference threshold (JND), which is the smallest change between two stimuli that you can notice.

mem: Absolute threshold: weakest intensity detected 50% of the time
JND: smallest change you can notice between two stimuli
Detection is hit or miss, never a sharp cutoff
d_6A_3.trap: Mixing up the absolute threshold (one stimulus) with the difference threshold (a change between two).
d_6A_3.plain: You whisper to a friend from far away and they hear you about half the time. That distance is the threshold.

ox: Not quite. Habituation is a decrease in response that happens in the brain when a harmless stimulus repeats. Nothing here involves an expectation, and the best match for a steady smell fading is the receptors themselves turning down.

Correct. Sensory adaptation is when receptors respond less to a stimulus that stays constant, like a steady perfume smell. After a few minutes, your smell receptors stop reporting it, and you stop noticing it.
Not quite. Nothing in the room damaged your nose. A threshold raised by damage wouldn't fade in over a few minutes, and it wouldn't bounce back when the smell changed. Adaptation does.

Not quite. Selective attention is choosing what to focus on, like listening to one voice in a noisy room. Here the smell fades on its own because the receptors turn down, not because you shifted your focus.

p: Sensory adaptation means receptors fire less when a stimulus stays the same. This frees you to notice changes instead of constant background, like the hum of a fridge or the feel of your clothes.

Habituation is different. It happens in the brain: you learn to ignore a harmless stimulus that keeps repeating, like a ticking clock. Both make you notice something less, but adaptation is at the receptor and habituation is in the brain.

mem: Sensory adaptation: receptors respond less to a constant stimulus
Habituation: the brain tunes out a repeated stimulus
Selective attention: choosing what to focus on
d_6A_6.trap: Picking habituation. On the MCAT, a constant stimulus fading at the receptor is adaptation.
d_6A_6.plain: You walk into a bakery and smell fresh bread. A few minutes later your nose stops reporting it, like a friend who gets bored of telling you the same news.

fig.cap: The basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base (high frequencies) and wide and floppy at the apex (low frequencies).
fig.alt: Unrolled cochlea showing the frequency map from base to apex.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. Hair cells in the organ of Corti bend against the tectorial membrane. That opens ion channels, the hair cells depolarize, and the movement becomes a neural signal. That's transduction.
Not quite. The ossicles, three tiny ear bones, boost the vibration and push on the oval window, not the round window. They only pass along mechanical movement. They don't turn it into nerve signals.
Not quite. Photoreceptors are the light-sensing cells in the retina of the eye. The cochlea uses hair cells to detect sound.
Not quite. The tympanic membrane, or eardrum, only vibrates when sound hits it. It doesn't fire action potentials. The first nerve signals come from the hair cells in the cochlea.

concept.t: How hearing turns sound into nerve signals
p: Transduction means converting one kind of energy into nerve signals. Sound is a mechanical vibration. The eardrum and the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) carry it inward as movement only. The stapes pushes on the oval window, the opening into the cochlea.

Inside the cochlea, fluid waves move the basilar membrane. Hair cells in the organ of Corti ride on it, and their hairs bend against the tectorial membrane above. That bending opens ion channels and creates the neural signal.

mem: Transduction happens in the hair cells of the organ of Corti
Ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes): mechanical boost only
The stapes pushes on the oval window
d_6A_9.trap: Thinking the eardrum or ossicles do the converting. They only move mechanically.
d_6A_9.plain: The eardrum and bones are like drumsticks passing a beat along. The hair cells are the microphone that turns the beat into an electrical signal.

fig.cap: The absolute threshold is the intensity detected on 50% of trials. Weber's law: the just-noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the starting intensity.
fig.alt: Psychometric function and Weber's law lines for weight and brightness.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Illustrative values.

ox: Not quite. This describes the difference threshold, also called the just noticeable difference (JND). That's the smallest change between two stimuli you can notice. The absolute threshold asks a different question: what's the weakest stimulus you can notice at all?
Not quite. The point where a stimulus starts to hurt is the pain threshold. That's a separate idea. The absolute threshold is about the faintest stimulus you can detect, not when it becomes painful.
Correct. The absolute threshold is the lowest intensity a person detects on 50% of trials. Detection near this level is hit or miss, so researchers use the halfway point as the cutoff.

Not quite. At very faint levels, your nervous system's random background activity makes detection hit or miss. The same faint stimulus is caught on some trials and missed on others. Requiring 100% would push the threshold well above the faintest level you can really sense, so 50% is the standard.

p: The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus (the faintest light, the softest sound) that you can detect. It answers the question: is anything there at all?

Detection near that level isn't all or nothing. Your nervous system always has some random background activity, called noise. So the same faint stimulus is noticed on some trials and missed on others. That's why researchers define the absolute threshold as the intensity detected on half (50%) of trials.
Keep it separate from the difference threshold (the JND). The JND is about noticing a change between two stimuli, like telling whether one sound is louder than another.

mem: Absolute threshold: weakest stimulus detected 50% of the time
JND: smallest change you can notice between two stimuli
Pain threshold is a different idea
x6A_001.trap: Picking 100%. Near threshold, no faint stimulus is caught every single time.
x6A_001.plain: Think of a friend whispering from across a room. Some tries you catch it, some you don't. The distance where you catch it half the time is your threshold.

fig.cap: The absolute threshold is the intensity detected on 50% of trials. Weber's law: the just-noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the starting intensity.
fig.alt: Psychometric function and Weber's law lines for weight and brightness.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Illustrative values.

ox: Not quite. This flips the meaning of the numbers. A larger Weber fraction (0.08) means you need a bigger change, compared with the starting level, before you notice. So brightness is judged less precisely, not more. It's easy to read a bigger number as better, but here it's worse.

Correct. A Weber fraction of 0.02 means a 2% change in weight is noticeable. Brightness needs 0.08, which is an 8% change. Needing a smaller change to notice a difference means finer judgment, so people pick up proportionally smaller changes in weight.

Not quite. Weber fractions come from difference thresholds, the smallest change you can notice between two stimuli. The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus you can detect at all. These numbers tell you nothing about that.

Not quite. Sensory adaptation is when a sense stops responding as much to a steady stimulus, like no longer noticing a smell. Weber fractions don't measure adaptation, so they can't tell you which sense adapts faster.

p: Weber's law says the change you need to notice a difference grows with the starting intensity. Adding 1 gram to a 10-gram letter is easy to feel; adding 1 gram to a 10-kilogram bag is not. What stays about the same is the proportion: JND ÷ starting intensity. That ratio is the Weber fraction.

Each sense has its own Weber fraction. A small fraction means you notice tiny relative changes, so that sense is more sensitive to differences. A large fraction means you need a big relative change before you notice.
To compare two fractions, turning them into percents helps: multiply by 100. The sense with the smaller percent is the sharper one.

fm.v: Weight fraction = 0.02 (no units, it's a ratio); brightness fraction = 0.08; which is more sensitive = ?

Weber fraction = JND ÷ starting intensity

Wrong. Feature detection is the bottom-up step of picking out lines and edges. Trap: mixing this with expectation-driven reading.

Bottom-up = raw features to perception

Wrong. Continuity prefers smooth, continuous lines or paths. Trap: dots in a row can suggest a line, but here grouping is by closeness.

Wrong. Change blindness is missing a change in a scene. Nothing changed here. Trap: confusing attention-related terms.

Stage 1: θ; Stage 2: spindles and K-complexes
Stage 3: delta waves, slow-wave sleep

Retro means backward, pro means forward. Ask: which memory is being blocked? If the old one is blocked, it is retroactive.

Proactive = old blocks new (forward)
Decay = fading from time alone; source amnesia = forgetting where you learned it

fig.cap: Stress depends on appraisal (threat? can I cope?); coping is problem-focused or emotion-focused.

ox: Not quite. Problem-focused coping goes after the cause of the stress, like making a plan or fixing the problem. A loss can't be undone, so there's nothing to fix.
Correct. Meditation calms your feelings when the situation can't be changed. That's emotion-focused coping, and it's a healthy, helpful choice when the stressor is out of your control.
Not quite. The alarm stage is the body's first physical reaction to stress in Selye's model. It's something that happens to you, not a coping strategy you choose.
Not quite. Learned helplessness means giving up because past stress seemed impossible to control. Meditating to calm yourself is an active strategy, the opposite of giving up.

p: Coping is how we deal with stress. Problem-focused coping tackles the cause of the stress directly. Emotion-focused coping manages the feelings the stress brings up.

When the cause can't be changed, like a death, emotion-focused coping (meditation, talking it through, relaxation) is the fitting choice. When the cause can be changed, problem-focused coping usually works better.

mem: Problem-focused = change the stressor
Emotion-focused = manage the feelings
Emotion-focused fits stressors you can't control

d_6C_14.plain: If your ball rolls over a fence, you can go get it: that's fixing the problem. If your pet has died, you can't fix that, so you comfort yourself instead.

ox: Not quite. Safety, love and esteem are levels of Maslow's hierarchy of needs. Both theories talk about needs, which is what makes this tempting, but these aren't self-determination theory's three.

Not quite. Drive, incentive and arousal are names of separate motivation theories: drive-reduction theory, incentive theory and arousal theory. They aren't the three needs of self-determination theory.

Correct. Self-determination theory says people thrive and feel intrinsically motivated when they have autonomy (control over their choices), competence (feeling skilled) and relatedness (connection with others).
Not quite. Extrinsic motivation, intrinsic motivation and amotivation (no motivation) are types of motivation. They describe what drives behavior, not the needs that have to be met.

p: Self-determination theory says people are most motivated from the inside, called intrinsic motivation, when three needs are met. Autonomy: feeling in charge of your own choices. Competence: feeling skilled. Relatedness: feeling connected to others.
Outside rewards, called extrinsic motivation, can sometimes weaken inner motivation if they make people feel controlled and cut into their sense of autonomy.

mem: Three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness
Meeting them boosts intrinsic motivation
Maslow's levels are different: physiological, safety, love, esteem, self-actualization
d_6C_23.trap: Confusing these three needs with Maslow's levels or with types of motivation.
d_6C_23.plain: You enjoy a video game more when you picked it yourself, you're getting good at it, and you play it with friends.

Not quite. Vision isn't lost. The monkeys can see, but they have trouble recognizing what objects are (visual agnosia), so they treat things oddly, like mouthing them.
Not quite. The defining signs are emotional and behavioral: tameness, no fear, mouthing objects. Trouble forming new declarative memories on its own is linked more to hippocampal damage.
Correct. This is Klüver-Bucy syndrome: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality (putting things in the mouth) and hypersexuality.

p: The amygdala is a small almond-shaped structure deep in the temporal lobe. It processes fear and aggression and helps judge whether something is a threat.

Removing both temporal lobes, including the amygdala, causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome. Animals become calm and fearless, put things in their mouths (hyperorality) and show more sexual behavior (hypersexuality).

mem: Amygdala = fear and aggression
Klüver-Bucy: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality, hypersexuality
Hippocampus = forming new declarative memories

ox: Not quite. Sensory, perceptual and motor describe how you take in a stimulus, make sense of it, and move in response. They're about processing information in general, not about what makes up an emotional experience.

Not quite. Conscious, preconscious and unconscious are Freud's levels of awareness: what you're aware of now, what you could bring to mind, and what's hidden. They say nothing about how an emotion is built.
Correct. An emotion has a physiological part (heart rate, sweating), a cognitive part (how you judge the situation and how it feels), and a behavioral part (facial expressions and actions).

Not quite. 'Primary' and 'secondary' show up in appraisal theory (primary appraisal asks 'Does this matter to me?', secondary asks 'Can I cope?') and in learning (primary reinforcers like food are rewarding from birth; secondary ones like money are learned). None of these are the parts of an emotion.

concept.t: The three parts of an emotion
p: Psychologists describe an emotion as having three parts. The physiological part is the body's reaction, like a racing heart, sweaty palms or fast breathing. These are mostly run automatically by the autonomic nervous system.

The cognitive part is what happens in your mind: how you size up the situation and the feeling you experience. The behavioral part is what others can see: your facial expression, your tone of voice, and what you do, like smiling, yelling or running away.

mem: Physiological = body changes inside
Cognitive = thoughts, judgment, feeling
Behavioral = expressions and actions
x6C_001.trap: Picking Freud's three levels of awareness just because they also come in threes.
x6C_001.plain: A big dog runs at you. Your stomach drops (body), you think 'that dog could bite me' (mind), and you back away fast (action).

ox: Not quite. The cognitive part is the judgment and feeling inside your head. Nobody can see it directly, but anyone can see a smile or a clenched fist.

Not quite. The physiological part means internal body changes, like a faster heart rate, higher blood pressure or sweating. Facial and hand movements that others can see are outward expressions, so they count as behavior. This is the tempting near-miss.
Not quite. Perception is how you interpret what your senses pick up. It's not one of the three parts of an emotion.
Correct. Smiling, frowning and clenching your fists are expressions and actions other people can observe. That's the behavioral part of emotion.

p: The behavioral part of emotion is what shows on the outside: facial expressions, posture, gestures, tone of voice and actions. Other people can observe it directly.

The physiological part happens inside the body, mostly automatically: heart rate, blood pressure, sweating, breathing. You'd need a monitor to measure most of it. The cognitive part is the judgment and feeling in your mind.

mem: Behavioral = expressions and actions you can see
Physiological = automatic changes inside the body
Cognitive = inner judgment and feeling
x6C_003.trap: Calling facial muscle movements physiological. Movements you can see are behavioral.
x6C_003.plain: Behavior is whatever a camera could film. Physiology is what you'd need a heart monitor to pick up.

ox: Not quite. Groupthink happens when members hide their doubts to keep the group in agreement, which can lead to bad decisions. Nothing here suggests anyone held back doubts; the group just leaned harder in its starting direction.
Correct. Group polarization is when discussion pushes a group further in the direction it already leaned. Moderately cautious investors became much more cautious.

Not quite. Conformity to an external norm means matching a standard that comes from outside the group. Here the group moved further along its own starting direction, with no outside standard involved.
Not quite. Social loafing is putting in less effort when working in a group because your share is hidden. It doesn't change people's opinions.

p: Group polarization means group discussion makes the group's average opinion more extreme in the direction it already leaned. If members lean cautious, they get more cautious. If they lean risky, they get riskier.

Two things drive it: hearing new arguments for the side most people already favor, and wanting to seem at least as committed as everyone else. Groups don't always move to the middle; often they move to the edge.

mem: Polarization: the starting lean gets stronger
Groupthink: doubts hidden to keep harmony
Social loafing: less effort in groups
Groups don't always moderate
d_7B_5.trap: Assuming groups always settle on a moderate view.
d_7B_5.plain: If everyone in the room mildly likes pizza, after talking it over for an hour, everyone is suddenly crazy about pizza.

ox: Not quite. The contact hypothesis says contact between groups can reduce prejudice under the right conditions, like equal status and shared goals. It doesn't explain boosting self-esteem by favoring your own group.
Correct. Social identity theory says the groups you belong to are part of your self-concept. Seeing your own group as better than others (ingroup bias) raises your self-esteem.
Not quite. The Barnum effect is accepting vague, general descriptions, like horoscopes, as accurate about you personally. It has nothing to do with groups.
Not quite. Self-perception theory says we figure out our attitudes by watching our own behavior: 'I keep going to the gym, so I must like exercise.' It isn't about comparing groups.

p: Social identity theory says part of who you are comes from the groups you belong to. Your ingroup is your own group. An outgroup is any group you're not part of.

To feel good about yourself, you may see your ingroup as better than outgroups. That's ingroup bias. A related bias is outgroup homogeneity: seeing members of other groups as all alike while seeing your own group as full of different individuals.

mem: Group membership feeds self-concept and self-esteem
Ingroup bias: favoring your own group
Outgroup homogeneity: seeing other groups as all alike
Contact hypothesis: reducing prejudice
d_7B_21.trap: Missing that group membership feeds self-esteem and grabbing a similar-sounding theory instead.
d_7B_21.plain: Fans think their team is the best one in the league. When the team wins, the fans feel good about themselves too.

ox: Not quite. Instinctual drives come from Freud's id, the part of the mind full of basic urges. Cooley's idea is social: it's about other people, not inner drives.

Not quite. Comparing your real self to an ideal self comes from Carl Rogers and from self-discrepancy theory. Cooley focused on how you imagine others judge you, not an inner ideal. The word 'only' is also a clue.
Correct. In Cooley's looking-glass self, we picture how others see us, picture how they judge us, and build our self-concept from that.
Not quite. Noticing your own body's arousal, like a racing heart, is part of emotion theories such as James-Lange and Schachter-Singer. It isn't how Cooley said the self-concept forms.

p: Your self-concept is your picture of who you are. Cooley said it comes largely from other people, who act like a mirror (a 'looking glass').

It happens in three steps. You imagine how you appear to others. You imagine how they judge you. Then you feel and think about yourself based on that. Note that it's what you imagine they think, which may not be what they really think.

mem: Looking-glass self: imagining others' judgments (Cooley)
Mead: stages of role-taking (play, game, generalized other)
Rogers: ideal self vs real self
Freud: id, ego, superego
d_7B_22.trap: Mixing up Cooley's imagined judgment of others with Mead's stages of role-taking.
d_7B_22.plain: It's like deciding you're funny because you picture your friends laughing at your jokes.

ox: Not quite. The fundamental attribution error is blaming other people's behavior on their personality while ignoring the situation. It's about judging others, not shaping your own image.
Correct. Impression management means deliberately controlling how others see you. Dressing well and stressing your strengths in a job interview is exactly that.

Not quite. Stereotype threat is doing worse on a task because you're worried about confirming a negative stereotype about your group. This candidate is acting on purpose to look good, not struggling under that worry.
Not quite. Deindividuation is losing self-awareness in a crowd or when you feel anonymous. This candidate is very self-aware and thinking carefully about how she looks.

p: Impression management, or self-presentation, is the effort to control how other people see you. It includes how you dress, how you speak and what you choose to mention or leave out.

Goffman described social life like a play: 'front stage' is how we act in front of an audience, and 'back stage' is where we relax. Impression management isn't always lying. It can be honest and still careful about what to show.

mem: Impression management: controlling how others see you
It can be honest, not only deceptive
Deindividuation: anonymity lowers self-awareness
Stereotype threat: fear of confirming a negative stereotype
d_7B_25.trap: Thinking impression management always means lying.
d_7B_25.plain: It's like tidying your room before a friend comes over so they see your best side.

ox: Not quite. The fundamental attribution error is explaining someone's behavior by their personality and ignoring the situation. No behavior is being explained here.
Not quite. The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve. It doesn't involve one trait spreading to others.
Correct. The halo effect is when one good trait, like attractiveness, makes you assume other good traits, like competence and honesty.
Not quite. Self-serving bias is taking credit for your own successes and blaming outside causes for your failures. It's about your own outcomes, not judging someone else.

p: The halo effect is a shortcut in how we judge people. One positive trait, like good looks or a friendly smile, makes us assume the person is good in other ways too.

It's a bias about one individual, not a whole group. Attractive people are often rated as smarter, kinder and more trustworthy without any evidence. The reverse, where one bad trait makes everything look worse, is sometimes called the horn effect.

mem: Halo effect: one good trait spreads to others
Attractive people get assumed competent and honest
Stereotyping is about groups; halo is about one person
Reverse: horn effect
d_7B_26.trap: Calling it stereotyping or the attribution error. The key is one trait spreading to others.
d_7B_26.plain: If a kid has the neatest handwriting, the teacher might guess the kid is also smart and well-behaved.

fig.cap: Ratio schedules give higher response rates than interval schedules. FR shows a pause after each reward, FI a 'scallop', and variable schedules steady responding; VR is the most resistant to extinction.
fig.alt: Cumulative response records for VR, FR, VI and FI schedules.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph (schematic shapes, not data).

r: Scalloped; speeds up near reward time

ox: Not quite. A fixed-ratio schedule pays after the same number of responses every time, like a free coffee after every 10. It gives bursts of responding with a pause after each reward. Slot machine payouts are unpredictable, not fixed.

Not quite. A fixed-interval schedule pays for the first response after a set amount of time. Responding speeds up as the time nears, which looks like a scallop on a graph. Slot machines depend on pulls, not time.

Not quite. A variable-interval schedule pays after unpredictable amounts of time, like checking for a text. Slot machines depend on the number of pulls, and variable-interval schedules give slower, steady responding.

Correct. Slot machines pay after an unpredictable number of pulls. That's a variable-ratio schedule. It produces high, steady responding and is very hard to extinguish, because the next pull could always be the one.

p: A schedule of reinforcement is the rule for when a behavior gets rewarded. Ratio schedules count responses. Interval schedules count time passing. Fixed means the requirement stays the same; variable means it changes unpredictably.

Variable ratio produces the highest, steadiest responding and is the hardest to extinguish. Fixed ratio gives bursts with pauses after each reward. Fixed interval gives a scallop, slow after a reward and faster as the time nears. Variable interval gives slow, steady responding.

mem: Variable ratio: unpredictable count, highest steady rate
Fixed ratio: bursts, then pauses
Fixed interval: scallop; variable interval: slow and steady

fig.cap: Responses to a repeated harmless stimulus fall (habituation) and return to a new stimulus (dishabituation); an intense event raises responding to many stimuli (sensitization).
fig.alt: Habituation, dishabituation and sensitization response curves.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph (schematic shapes, not data).

ox: Not quite. Extinction is when a learned response fades because the cue keeps showing up without the thing it used to predict. Reacting to a loud train was never learned that way. It's a built-in startle, so extinction doesn't apply.
Correct. The trains are harmless and keep coming, so the student's reaction shrinks over time. A drop in response to a repeated, harmless stimulus is habituation. The student simply stops noticing.
Not quite. Sensitization is when your reaction gets bigger, usually after something intense or painful. Here the reaction got smaller, so it's the opposite.

Not quite. Stimulus discrimination means learning to react to one stimulus but not a similar one, like jumping at your own phone's ring but not someone else's. The student isn't telling sounds apart. He's just tuning one out.

p: Habituation is one of the simplest kinds of learning. When a stimulus (anything that triggers a reaction) keeps repeating and nothing bad happens, you react to it less and less.

It's called non-associative learning because nothing gets paired with anything else. You're learning about one stimulus on its own. It's useful: it frees your attention for things that might actually matter.

mem: Habituation: repeated harmless thing, smaller reaction
Sensitization: after something intense, bigger reaction
Both are non-associative (no pairing)
x7C_001.trap: Picking extinction because responding drops. Extinction needs a response that was first learned by pairing, and a startle to noise never was.

ox: Correct. The explosion was intense, and afterward the soldier reacts more to many different sounds. A bigger, widespread response after a strong stimulus is sensitization.
Not quite. Habituation is when a reaction gets smaller with repetition. The soldier is startling more, not less.
Not quite. Dishabituation is when a reaction you had tuned out suddenly comes back for that one stimulus. Nothing was tuned out here, and the jump in startle covers lots of unrelated sounds.

Not quite. Negative reinforcement means a behavior gets stronger because it takes away something unpleasant, like taking aspirin to remove a headache. No behavior is being rewarded by removing anything here.

p: Sensitization is when a strong or harmful stimulus makes you react more strongly afterward. Like habituation, it's non-associative: nothing is being paired with anything.
The key feature is that it spreads. After the intense event, you're more reactive to many different stimuli, even ones that have nothing to do with the original event. It usually wears off with time.

mem: Sensitization: intense event, bigger and broader reactions
Habituation: repeated harmless thing, smaller reaction
Dishabituation: a faded reaction to one thing comes back
x7C_003.trap: Picking dishabituation because the response goes up. Dishabituation is about one stimulus you had tuned out, not a jump across many sounds.
x7C_003.plain: After a loud thunderclap, you flinch at every creak in the house for the next hour.

fig.cap: Responses to a repeated harmless stimulus fall (habituation) and return to a new stimulus (dishabituation); an intense event raises responding to many stimuli (sensitization).

ox: Not quite. The babies looked longer at the new face. Longer looking means the new face caught their interest, so this shows a pull toward the new one, not the familiar one.
Not quite. Operant reinforcement needs a consequence after the behavior, like a reward for looking. Nothing happened after the babies looked, so there was no reinforcement.

Correct. Looking dropped for the repeated face and then rose again for the new face. The baby can only react to the new face as new if it can tell the two apart. So the infants can discriminate between the faces.
Not quite. Sensitization would make the babies react more to everything. Their looking at the repeated face went down, which is the opposite.

New thing: looking rises (dishabituation)
Rise means the baby can tell them apart

x7C_004.plain: You zone out during the same commercial every time, but you look up when a new one comes on. That tells someone watching you that you noticed it was new.

ox: Correct. If a new stimulus can snap the response right back, the sense organs were never worn out. So the drop must have come from the brain learning to ignore the stimulus. That's habituation, and it's exactly what separates it from receptor-level adaptation.
Not quite. Habituation is a learned drop in responding that happens in the brain. It shows up with sounds, touch, smells and sights, so it isn't confined to the retina.

Not quite. This has it backwards. Being reversed by a new stimulus is the mark of habituation. Sensory adaptation happens in the receptors and recovers only after the stimulus has been gone for a while.
Not quite. Habituation needs no reward at all. Simply repeating a harmless stimulus is enough to make the response shrink.

Habituation: the brain stops caring
Quick comeback with a new stimulus means habituation

Not quite. Reaction formation is a Freudian defense mechanism: acting the opposite of an impulse you find unacceptable, like being overly nice to someone you secretly resent. Nothing like that is happening here.
Not quite. Self-efficacy is your belief that you can succeed at a particular task. This story is about how she came to see herself through other people's eyes, not her confidence in doing a task.
Not quite. Moratorium is one of Marcia's identity statuses: actively exploring options without committing yet. It doesn't describe how other people's judgments shape your self-view.

p: Cooley said we form our self-image as if looking into a mirror made of other people. There are three steps: we imagine how we appear to others, we imagine how they judge us, and we feel and react to that judgment.
The teenager keeps hearing that she's artistic and gets praise for her drawings. She takes in that view and starts to see herself as an artistic person.
