Correct. In Mead's play stage, children take on one specific role at a time, like a doctor talking to a patient. They can't yet juggle several roles at once.

Not quite. The game stage requires keeping track of many roles at once, like players on a team, and understanding the generalized other, society's shared expectations. The question says she can't do that yet.
Not quite. Formal operational is Jean Piaget's last stage of cognitive development, when abstract thinking appears in adolescence. It isn't part of Mead's theory.

p: Mead described three stages. Preparatory: copying others without understanding. Play: acting out one person's role at a time. Game: understanding many roles at once and the generalized other, meaning society's shared expectations.
Playing doctor means taking on one role at a time, so this child is in the play stage. Team sports, where she'd need to track everyone's role, belong to the game stage.

Correct. Blaming an unfair test and a professor's dislike puts the cause outside the student. Thinking this way across many situations is an external locus of control.
Not quite. High self-efficacy is a belief that you can succeed through your own actions. Blaming outside forces suggests the opposite: a feeling that outcomes aren't in your hands.
Not quite. Self-discrepancy theory is about gaps between who you are (actual self) and who you hope to be (ideal self). Nothing in this story involves that comparison.

p: Locus of control is where you believe the causes of events lie. With an internal locus, you credit your own effort and choices. With an external locus, you credit luck, other people or circumstances.

This student blames the test and the professor, and does so across situations. That consistent pattern is an external locus of control. People with an internal locus tend to cope better and achieve more, since they believe effort makes a difference.

mem: Internal locus: I cause my outcomes
External locus: luck, others or fate cause them
Self-efficacy is different: belief in your ability at a task
d_8A_6.trap: Reading blame of others as high self-esteem. It signals an external locus, not confidence.
d_8A_6.plain: If you always say the dog ate your homework, you see things as happening to you, not because of you.

ox: Correct. Self-concept is everything you believe and know about yourself: your traits, roles, values and so on. It's the full description of who you think you are.

Not quite. Self-esteem is the judgment of how worthy you are, a feeling about yourself. It's one piece, not the whole set of beliefs. It's easy to mix up a description of yourself with how you rate that description.
Not quite. Self-efficacy is believing you can succeed at a particular task, like 'I can pass this exam.' It's about ability in specific situations, not your overall picture of yourself.

Not quite. Identity foreclosure is one of James Marcia's identity statuses. It describes someone who commits to an identity without exploring other options, like taking on a parent's career plans without question.

p: Self-concept is everything you believe about yourself: 'I'm a student, I'm funny, I'm a night owl.' It's a description, not a judgment.

Self-esteem is how you feel about that self, your sense of overall worth. Self-efficacy is narrower still: your belief that you can handle a specific task. All three start with 'self,' so focus on what each one does: describe, judge, or predict success.

Self-esteem: how much I value myself
Self-efficacy: I can do this task
Foreclosure: commitment without exploring

x8A_001.plain: Self-concept is the description of you on a report card. Self-esteem is the overall grade you give yourself.

ox: Not quite. A self-schema is an organized set of beliefs about yourself in one area, like 'I'm a good athlete.' It describes what you're like. It doesn't measure how much you value yourself.
Correct. Self-esteem is your overall feeling of worth: how much you like and value yourself as a whole person.
Not quite. Self-efficacy is confidence that you can do a specific task. You can feel sure you'll ace math and still have low self-esteem overall. 'Can I do it?' isn't the same as 'Am I worth it?'
Not quite. Locus of control is whether you think outcomes come from you (internal) or from outside forces like luck (external). It says nothing about how much you value yourself.

p: Self-esteem is the feeling part of the self: your overall judgment of your own worth. High self-esteem means you generally like and respect yourself.

Several other 'self' ideas are narrower. A self-schema is a belief about yourself in one area. Self-efficacy is confidence in doing one kind of task. Locus of control is about who or what you think controls outcomes. Only self-esteem is a global worth judgment.

mem: Self-esteem: overall worth
Self-efficacy: confidence in a specific task
Self-schema: a belief about yourself in one area
Locus of control: where you think outcomes come from
x8A_002.trap: Choosing self-efficacy because both sound like feeling good about yourself. Efficacy is task-specific; esteem is global.
x8A_002.plain: Self-esteem is the grade you give yourself as a whole person, not the grade on one test.

ox: Not quite. A situational attribution blames things outside the person, like luck, traffic or a hard test. Pointing to someone's traits is the opposite of that.
Not quite. External causes are situational ones, and traits live inside the person, so the two words clash. "Stable-external" also isn't the standard name for a trait explanation.

Not quite. Self-serving bias is a pattern: you credit yourself when things go well and blame circumstances when they go badly. It's a tendency in how you pick causes, not the label for every explanation that mentions a trait.
Correct. A dispositional attribution says the cause is inside the person: their traits, abilities, effort or character. Another word for it is internal attribution.

p: An attribution is simply the reason you give for someone's behavior. Psychologists sort those reasons by where they put the cause.
A dispositional (internal) attribution points at the person: "he's late because he's lazy." A situational (external) attribution points at the circumstances: "he's late because traffic was terrible."
Biases like the self-serving bias are patterns in which kind of attribution people tend to pick. They aren't extra categories of attribution.

mem: Dispositional = internal = about the person
Situational = external = about the circumstances
Self-serving bias is a pattern, not a type
x8B_001.trap: Mixing up the words disposition and situation, or grabbing self-serving bias because it sounds related.
x8B_001.plain: Your friend shows up late. "He's lazy" is about him. "Traffic was awful" is about the situation.

ox: Not quite. Low consensus means other people don't act this way. Low distinctiveness means this person acts this way with lots of things. High consistency means they always do. Put together, that says the cause is the person, which is a dispositional attribution.

Correct. High consensus means everyone reacts this way. High distinctiveness means this person reacts this way only to this one thing. High consistency means it happens every time. When everyone does it, only here, and reliably, the situation is what's causing it.

Not quite. Low consistency means the behavior doesn't happen reliably, which points to a one-time fluke, not a clear cause. Low distinctiveness also means the person acts this way in lots of places, which points away from this particular situation.

Not quite. Low consensus means other people don't act this way, which hints at the person, not the situation. And low consistency means it doesn't happen reliably, so there's no stable cause to name at all.

p: Kelley's model lists three clues people use to explain behavior. Consensus asks whether other people act the same way. Distinctiveness asks whether this person acts this way only toward this one thing. Consistency asks whether it happens every time.

High on all three points to the situation or the thing being reacted to. Low consensus and low distinctiveness with high consistency points to the person. Low consistency on its own suggests a passing, one-off circumstance.

mem: High, high, high = the situation
Low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency = the person
Low consistency = a one-time fluke
x8B_003.trap: Flipping which pattern means person and which means situation. High distinctiveness means "only in this situation", so it pushes you toward the situation.
x8B_003.plain: If every kid hates one scary movie, your friend hates only that movie, and he hates it every time, the movie is the problem, not your friend.

fig.cap: Each attribution bias places the cause differently: others' acts on their disposition (FAE), my failures on the situation (self-serving), out-group successes on luck (ultimate attribution error).

ox: Not quite. Actor-observer bias is when you blame the situation for your own behavior but blame character for other people's. That needs a self-versus-other comparison. Here, everyone is only judging someone else.

Not quite. Cognitive dissonance is the uncomfortable feeling you get when your own beliefs and actions don't match. The participants are judging another person's essay, not wrestling with their own inconsistency.
Not quite. A self-fulfilling prophecy happens when an expectation changes how someone actually behaves, so the expectation comes true. Nothing in this study changes the writer's behavior.

Correct. The participants assume the writer believes what the essay says, even though a coin flip chose the side. Inferring an attitude that matches behavior despite an obvious outside cause is correspondence bias, another name for the fundamental attribution error.

p: Correspondence bias is assuming that what someone does matches who they are inside, even when the situation forced the behavior.

It's the same idea as the fundamental attribution error (FAE): overrating character and underrating circumstances when explaining other people. In this classic essay study, the coin flip is the obvious situational cause, and observers still ignore it.

mem: Correspondence bias = fundamental attribution error
It happens even when the outside pressure is obvious
Classic proof: the assigned-essay study

x8B_006.plain: An actor plays a villain in a movie, and a kid decides the actor must be mean in real life.

ox: Not quite. Cutting down mental effort is the job of heuristics (mental shortcuts) and stereotypes. The self-serving bias is driven by wanting to feel good about yourself, not by saving brainpower.
Correct. Crediting yourself for success and blaming circumstances for failure keeps your self-esteem up. That self-protection is the main explanation for why the bias exists.
Not quite. A bias pulls your judgment away from reality. Giving yourself credit for every win and none of the blame for losses makes your view of yourself less accurate, not more.
Not quite. Favoring your in-group is the group-serving bias: credit your group for wins, blame outside causes for its losses. The self-serving bias is about protecting the individual.

p: The self-serving bias is a kind of motivated reasoning. That just means your mind bends its explanations in the direction that makes you feel better.
Crediting yourself for wins and blaming the situation for losses keeps your self-worth high. The cost is accuracy: you see yourself a bit more kindly than the facts support.

mem: Job: protect and boost self-esteem
Cost: less accuracy
Group version: group-serving bias
x8B_009.trap: Picking "increasing accuracy". A bias pulls you away from reality, so it can't make you more accurate.
x8B_009.plain: A kid says "I scored the goal" when he scores, and "the wind made me miss" when he doesn't. Both explanations protect his pride.

ox: Not quite. Stereotype threat is the worry that you'll confirm a negative stereotype about your group, which can drag down your performance on a task. It doesn't explain how outside observers judge a crime victim.

Not quite. Self-serving bias is about explaining your own successes and failures in a way that protects your self-esteem. The participants are judging someone else's misfortune, so their own outcomes aren't at stake.

Not quite. The halo effect is when one good trait (like good looks) makes us assume other good traits (like kindness). It doesn't flip around when a crime goes unsolved, and it has nothing to do with beliefs about fairness.

Correct. An unsolved attack on an innocent person threatens the belief that the world is fair. Since the wrong can't be fixed, people fix their view of it instead: they decide the victim is less worthy, so the outcome seems more deserved.

concept.t: Just-world belief and blaming the victim
p: People with a strong just-world belief expect good people to be rewarded and bad people to be punished. It's comforting, because it makes the world feel predictable and safe.

When an innocent person suffers and nobody is punished, that comfort breaks. One way people repair it is victim derogation: lowering their opinion of the victim, so the suffering looks deserved. The effect is strongest when justice can't be restored.

mem: Just-world belief: people get what they deserve
Threatened belief leads to devaluing the victim
Strongest when the wrong can't be fixed
x8B_011.trap: Choosing self-serving bias just because it names a bias. Ask whose outcome is being explained: here it's the victim's, not the participants'.
x8B_011.plain: A good kid gets hurt and nobody is blamed. A child who believes life is always fair decides that kid must not have been so good after all.

ox: Correct. She earned the title through residency and board certification. A status you gain through your own effort is an achieved status.

Not quite. A master status is one status that overshadows all the others in how people see someone. Nothing here says her job drowns out everything else about her.
Not quite. "Primary" describes a type of group, a small, close one like a family. It isn't a type of status.

p: A status is a position in society, like student, mother or surgeon. An achieved status is one you gain through effort, choices or merit, like earning a degree.
An ascribed status is assigned to you without effort, usually at birth. A master status is a separate idea: it's any status that overshadows all your others in how people see you.

Ascribed = handed to you

Correct. His ex-offender status overshadows his degree and his work history. A status that dominates all the others like that is a master status.

p: A master status is the one status that overrides all the others and shapes how people treat you. It can be positive, like "famous athlete," or negative, like "ex-offender."
How it was gained doesn't matter. What makes it master is that it dominates. This one is actually achieved, since it came from his own actions.

It can be ascribed or achieved

Not quite. A master status is the one status that overshadows all the others in how people see you. Nothing here says her job dominates her identity.

Not quite. Role exit is the process of leaving a role. He hasn't left anything, and it isn't a type of status anyway.

Ascribed examples: age, sex, race, royal birth. Achieved examples: surgeon, college graduate.

ox: Correct. Status inconsistency means a person holds statuses with very different prestige. Physician ranks high, her group membership is looked down on by some, so people treat her in mixed ways.
Not quite. Role exit means leaving a role. She's still a physician, so nothing has been left.

Not quite. Her physician status is achieved, but "achieved master status" doesn't describe a clash between statuses. That clash is the whole point of the question.

Not quite. Demographic transition theory describes how a country's birth and death rates change as it develops. It has nothing to do with everyday interaction.

Meaning isn't built into the symbol. People negotiate it, so the same gesture can be read differently by different people.

mem: Symbolic interactionism: micro, meaning from symbols
Functionalism and conflict theory: macro
The same symbol can carry different meanings

ox: Not quite. This describes biological determinism, the view that categories are fixed facts society simply finds. Constructionism says the opposite.
Correct. Social constructionism holds that categories like adolescence get their meaning from shared agreement, so they vary across societies and eras.
Not quite. This describes rational choice theory, where people weigh personal costs and benefits.
Not quite. This is a narrow conflict-theory claim. The word 'only' is a warning sign, and it says nothing about how categories get their meaning.

p: Social constructionism says many things we treat as real, such as money or adolescence, have meaning because people agree on it together.
Because people make these meanings, they differ across cultures and over time. Constructed doesn't mean fake: these ideas still have real effects on people's lives.

mem: Meanings are created by shared agreement
Categories vary across cultures and history
Constructed doesn't mean unreal

d_9A_6.plain: A playground game's rules exist because the kids agree on them. Different playgrounds have different rules.

Not quite. A reference group is a group you compare yourself to when judging your own behavior or status. It says nothing about rejecting values.

A counterculture goes further. It actively rejects the main culture's norms and builds a way of life against them. The key idea is opposition.

Not quite. Rationalization spreads formal organizations and bureaucracy rather than shrinking them.

The four features: efficiency (the fastest way), predictability (the same everywhere), calculability (numbers and quantity over quality) and control (rules and technology direct people).

Four parts: efficiency, predictability, calculability, control

ox: Not quite. Conflict theory sees society as groups competing over limited resources, with some winning and others losing. That's the opposite of organs cooperating. It's tempting because it's also a big-picture theory.
Not quite. Symbolic interactionism zooms in on small, face-to-face moments and the meanings people give things. It doesn't treat society as one big organism.
Correct. Functionalism, which grew out of Durkheim's work, treats society like a body. Each institution is an organ with a job, and together they keep the whole in balance.
Not quite. Rational choice theory looks at one person comparing costs and benefits before deciding. It says nothing about society working like a living body.

p: Functionalism is a macro theory, meaning it looks at society as a whole rather than at individual people. It pictures society as a system of connected parts, the way a body is made of organs.
Each part, like the family, schools or government, has a function: a job that helps the whole system stay stable. If one part changes, the others shift to bring things back into balance.

mem: Functionalism: society as an organism that stays stable
It grew out of Durkheim's work
Conflict theory: competition, not cooperation

ox: Not quite. Even at replacement fertility, a young population keeps growing for decades because so many people are still entering their childbearing years. That's population momentum, so zero growth doesn't happen immediately.
Correct. A TFR of about 2.1 replaces the two parents, with a small extra amount for children who die before they're old enough to have kids.
